• D. Boiling: Highly effective but less economical, especially for large volumes and in disaster situations due to fuel requirements.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While checking for water contamination in a village tank, which of the following parameters, if found, would indicate that the water quality does not meet defined standards and guidelines?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cadmium 0.3 mg/litre

Water standards and guidelines:

• Colour < 15 TCU (5 Hazen)
• Turbidity < 5 NTU
• Hardness < 100–300 mg/L
• pH: 6.5 – 8.5
• Total dissolved solids (TDS) < 300 mg/L
• Fluoride < 1 mg/L (0.5 – 0.8 mg/L)
• Nitrates < 45 mg/L
• Nitrites < 3 mg/L
• Cadmium ≤ 0.003 mg/L
• Gross alpha radiological activity < 0.5 Bq/L
• Gross beta radiological activity < 1.0 Bq/L

Thus cadmium 0.3 mg/L exceeds the safe limit by \~100 times.

Cadmium is a heavy metal contaminant that can cause:

Chronic exposure leads to Itai-itai disease, first reported in Japan.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While checking the immunization technique of an ANM worker, you observe that she has used cotton, a syringe, and a needle. After immunization, which of the following statements regarding biomedical waste disposal is correct?
options: Syringe with needle in black translucent container
Used vial in translucent white container
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cotton swab in yellow bag

Under Biomedical Waste Management Rules, cotton swabs contaminated with blood or body fluids are classified as soiled waste.

Soiled waste is disposed of in the yellow bag, which is meant for incineration or deep burial.

Sharps (needles) go in white translucent puncture-proof containers, glass vials in blue, and syringes (without needles) in red, making option C correct.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While numerous animals play a role in the transmission of rabies, dogs stand out as the most common ones. Moreover, the impact of this disease is often more in children. Given this understanding, what approach would be both economically efficient and rational to reduce the occurrence of rabies?
options: Testing all the dogs for rabies
Reduce stray dog population and vaccinate all dogs
Increase capacity of healthcare workers for surveillance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reduce stray dog population and vaccinate all dogs

Rabies is primarily transmitted by dogs, and children are disproportionately affected. The most cost-effective and rational strategy to reduce rabies incidence is source control, i.e., targeting the animal reservoir.

• Mass dog vaccination (≥70%) interrupts transmission.
• Control of stray dog population reduces human exposure.
• This approach is far more economical and effective than post-exposure management alone.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are employed at a primary health center (PHC) located in an area with a high risk of earthquakes. What actions would you take to ensure readiness for potential emergencies? A) Disaster preparedness by making sure all financial and other resources are available B) Increase public awareness through campaigns and loudspeakers C) Conduct a simulation for the disaster and assess the response D) Follow instructions given over the phone or radio by higher officials
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3

Disaster preparedness focuses on actions taken before a disaster to ensure an effective response.

This includes ensuring availability of resources (manpower, logistics, finances), raising public awareness about do’s and don’ts, and conducting mock drills or simulations to test preparedness and identify gaps.

Following instructions from higher authorities is part of the response phase, not preparedness, making 1, 2, and 3 the correct components.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presented to OPD of a PHC Watery diarrhoea having severe dehydration. Most likely causative agent underlying would be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rota virus

In children below 5 years, rotavirus is the most common cause of acute watery diarrhoea and is frequently associated with severe dehydration due to profuse fluid loss.

Rotavirus infects the enterocytes of the small intestine which causes destruction of intestinal epithelial cells, reduced absorption of fluids and increased intestinal secretion that results in Profuse watery diarrhoea.

Bacterial causes like Shigella and Salmonella typically produce inflammatory or dysenteric diarrhoea, while E. coli O157:H7 is more often linked to bloody diarrhoea and HUS rather than severe watery diarrhoea.

Rotavirus infection can be prevented by vaccination.

India includes the Rotavirus vaccine in the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with flaccid paralysis after consuming improperly stored, open canned food. Clostridium botulinum toxin exposure is suspected. Which of the following best describes the mode of transmission in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vehicle borne transmission

Understand that vehicle-borne transmission occurs when an infectious agent or its toxin is transmitted through a contaminated inanimate medium, such as food, water, milk, blood, or biological products. Foodborne botulism results from ingestion of preformed botulinum toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum in improperly preserved or canned foods, making it a classic example of vehicle-borne transmission.

Why not the other options?

• A. Direct transmission: Requires immediate person-to-person contact (e.g., touching, kissing, sexual contact); not applicable to botulism.
• B. Vector-borne transmission: Involves transmission through arthropods such as mosquitoes, ticks, or fleas; C. botulinum is not vector transmitted.
• D. Indirect transmission: A broad category that includes vehicle-borne, vector-borne, and airborne transmission. Vehicle-borne is the more specific and correct answer in this case.

| Mode of Transmission | Example

| -------------------- | -------

| Direct | Touch, sexual contact, droplet spread at close range

| Vehicle-borne | Botulism from canned food, Cholera from contaminated water, Hepatitis A from contaminated food

| Vector-borne | Malaria, Dengue, Plague

| Airborne | Tuberculosis, Measles, Varicella

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presented to Ayushman Arogya Mandir with blood pressure measurements of 148/93 and 153/99 on two separate occasions. What is the next step in management?
options: Admit the patient and give IV antihypertensives
Start the patient on Amlodipine 5mg per day and follow up after 1 month
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Start the patient on Amlodipine 5mg per day and follow up after 1 month

Blood pressure readings ≥140/90 mmHg on two separate occasions confirm hypertension.

As per NPCDCS / Ayushman Arogya Mandir guidelines, uncomplicated Stage 1–2 hypertension is managed at the primary level by initiating first-line antihypertensive therapy (e.g., Amlodipine 5 mg daily) with follow-up after 1 month for titration and monitoring.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A case control study is done to study the association between smoking and lung cancer. Which of the following is incorrect?
options: Controls are selected from the population from which cases arise
Multiple controls per case increase the statistical power
Matching the controls with cases will eliminate all confounders
The selection of the controls from the hospital will cause selection bias
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Matching the controls with cases will eliminate all confounders

In a case–control study, controls should be selected from the same source population as cases, and using multiple controls per case increases statistical power. Controls should reflect the exposure distribution of the population that produced the cases. Example- If lung cancer cases come from a city population, controls should also come from the same city population.Otherwise, selection bias occurs.

Hospital-based controls may introduce selection bias if their exposure pattern differs from the general population.

Matching helps control specific known confounders, but it cannot eliminate all confounding, especially from unknown or unmeasured variables, making option C incorrect.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A case-control study was conducted to assess the association between smoking and lung cancer in 200 subjects. The data are shown below. What is the odds ratio for lung cancer in smokers compared to non-smokers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6

Odds Ratio (OR) is the measure of association used in case-control studies and compares the odds of exposure among cases to the odds of exposure among controls. It is calculated using the cross-product ratio (ad/bc).

| | Lung Cancer (+) | Lung Cancer (−)

| --- | --------------- | ---------------

| Smoker | a = 80 | b = 40

| Non-smoker | c = 20 | d = 60

Odds Ratio (OR) = (a × d) / (b × c)

= (80 × 60) / (40 × 20)

= 4800 / 800 = 6

Thus, smokers have 6 times higher odds of developing lung cancer than non-smokers.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A city is divided into 5 economic zones, and individuals are randomly selected from each zone. Which sampling technique is used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stratified random sampling

• The population is divided into homogeneous strata.
• A random sample is taken from every stratum.
• Here, economic zones act as strata.
• Stratified sampling improves representativeness.

• It ensures all important subgroups are included.

• Cluster sampling randomly selects entire clusters.

• In cluster sampling, not every cluster is necessarily sampled.

• Simple random sampling does not involve grouping.
• Systematic sampling selects every kth individual.
• Strata = sample from each; Cluster = sample whole clusters.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A cohort study was carried out involving individuals who consumed green tea and those who did not, aiming to examine its impact on diabetes mellitus. The calculated risk ratio stood at 0.84. Which of the subsequent statements is accurate?
options: Green tea increases the risk of diabetes
Green tea decreases the risk of diabetes
Data insufficient to establish causal association
The value (0.84) tends to be close to 1, hence there is no effect
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Green tea decreases the risk of diabetes

A risk ratio (relative risk) of 0.84 indicates that the exposed group (green tea consumers) has 16% lower risk of developing diabetes compared to the unexposed group.

A value less than 1 signifies a protective effect, while a value greater than 1 indicates increased risk.

Although causality requires further evaluation, the correct interpretation of the given RR is that green tea consumption is associated with a reduced risk of diabetes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A cohort study was done with a sample size of 500, and 20 of them developed the disease over two years. Total person-time observed was 950 years. Calculate the incidence rate.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2.1 per 100 person-years

Incidence rate is calculated as the number of new cases divided by total person-time at risk.

Here, incidence rate = 20 ÷ 950 = 0.021 per person-year, which when expressed per 100 person-years equals 2.1 per 100 person-years.

Incidence rate uses person-time, not total population or duration alone, distinguishing it from cumulative incidence.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A community reports 100 deaths in one year. Of these, 8 deaths are due to tuberculosis. Calculate the Proportionate Mortality Rate (PMR) due to TB.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8%

• PMR indicates the proportion of all deaths due to a specific cause.
• Formula:

• TB deaths = 8.
• Total deaths = 100.
• PMR = 8/100 × 100 = 8%.
• PMR is not a mortality rate in the epidemiological sense.
• It does not measure the risk of dying.
• It only shows the relative contribution of a disease to total deaths.
• Denominator is total deaths, not population.
• Useful for identifying leading causes of mortality.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A hospital is comparing two treatment strategies for the same disease. Treatment A costs ₹5,000 and has a 70% success rate, whereas Treatment B costs ₹8,000 with an 85% success rate. Which of the following economic evaluation methods is most appropriate for comparing these interventions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cost-effectiveness analysis

Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) is used when interventions are compared based on cost (monetary units) and clinical outcomes measured in natural units, such as treatment success, life-years gained, cases prevented, or blood pressure reduction. Since the outcome here is success rate (%), CEA is the appropriate method.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cost-benefit analysis: Both costs and benefits are expressed in monetary terms (e.g., ₹ saved), which is not the case here.
• C. Cost-utility analysis: Outcomes are measured in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), not simple treatment success.
• D. Cost-minimization analysis: Applicable only when both interventions have equivalent clinical effectiveness, which is not true here.

High-Yield Pearl:

The Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER) is calculated as: ICER = (Cost₂ − Cost₁) ÷ (Effect₂ − Effect₁)

In this example:

• Additional cost = ₹8,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹3,000
• Additional effectiveness = 85% − 70% = 15%

ICER = ₹3,000 ÷ 15 = ₹200 per 1% additional treatment success, making this a classic example of cost-effectiveness analysis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A housefly transmits any infectious agent by which of the following methods, most commonly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mechanical transmission

The housefly (Musca domestica) is the most important mechanical vector of disease. It transmits pathogens by passive transfer on its legs, body hairs, wings, mouthparts, and through contaminated vomitus and feces. Since the infectious agent does not multiply or undergo any developmental cycle within the fly, the mode of transmission is mechanical.

• Mechanical transmission: No multiplication or development of the pathogen in the vector. ⭐
• Housefly commonly transmits:

• Typhoid fever
• Cholera
• Bacillary dysentery
• Amoebiasis
• Acute diarrheal diseases

• Propagative transmission: Pathogen multiplies only in the vector (e.g., Yersinia pestis – Rat flea).
• Cyclo-developmental transmission: Pathogen develops but does not multiply (e.g., Wuchereria bancrofti – Mosquito).
• Cyclo-propagative transmission: Pathogen both develops and multiplies (e.g., Plasmodium – Female Anopheles mosquito).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient was admitted to the hospital with COVID-19 and died 15 days later due to the illness. His death was reported through the official health reporting system. According to surveillance definitions, this type of reporting represents which form of surveillance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Passive surveillance

Disease surveillance is the continuous systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health data for public health action.

Different surveillance methods are used depending on how data are collected.

In this case, the hospital reported the case through routine reporting channels, which is characteristic of passive surveillance.

Passive surveillance involves routine reporting of diseases and deaths by healthcare facilities to health authorities without active case search.

In this scenario, the COVID-19 death was reported through the official health reporting system, fitting the definition of passive surveillance.

India uses systems such as the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP).

IDSP collects:

• Weekly disease reports
• Outbreak alerts
• Laboratory data

Most reporting in IDSP is passive surveillance.

Active surveillance requires deliberate outreach and case finding, while sentinel and syndromic surveillance serve different monitoring purposes.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person meets with an accident and as a result of which, the person loses his/her right arm, because of which the person is not able to drive the car to reach his/her office, and has to hire a driver for the same. The given condition of the person is most appropriately classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Disability

The WHO ICIDH framework distinguishes:

• Impairment: Loss or abnormality of a body structure or function.

• Example: Loss of the right arm.

• Disability: Restriction or inability to perform an activity in the normal manner because of an impairment.

• Here, the person cannot drive a car because of the lost arm → Disability.

• Handicap: A disadvantage resulting from impairment/disability that limits a person’s social role or participation.

• Example: Difficulty obtaining or maintaining employment because of the disability.

• Disease: A pathological condition affecting the body.

Therefore, the inability to drive the car represents disability → C.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A public health researcher observes that nearly two-thirds of all stroke cases in a community are attributable to hypertension (HTN) and estimates that these cases could be prevented if hypertension were effectively controlled. This scenario best illustrates which of the following epidemiological measures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Population attributable risk

Population Attributable Risk (PAR) estimates the proportion or number of disease cases in the entire population that can be attributed to a specific risk factor and therefore could be prevented if that exposure were eliminated or adequately controlled.

In this question:

• The statement refers to all stroke cases in the community, not just among hypertensive individuals.
• It also states that these cases could be prevented if hypertension were controlled.

These are the defining features of Population Attributable Risk.

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Relative Risk: Compares the risk of disease in exposed versus unexposed individuals; it does not estimate preventable disease burden in the entire population.

B. Attributable Risk: Measures the excess risk due to an exposure among exposed individuals only.

C. Odds Ratio: Compares the odds of exposure between cases and controls and is primarily used in case-control studies. It does not quantify the preventable disease burden in a population.

High-yield point

• Attributable Risk (AR): Excess risk among the exposed population.
• Population Attributable Risk (PAR): Excess disease burden in the entire population due to an exposure and the proportion of disease that could be prevented by eliminating that exposure.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A research study finds that using mammography for breast cancer screening appears to improve outcomes by increasing 5-year survival rates. However, post-mortem data show no real reduction in overall mortality. This apparent improvement in survival, despite unchanged mortality, is an example of which of the following epidemiological biases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lead time bias

Lead time bias occurs when earlier detection through screening increases the measured survival time without actually delaying death.

Mammography detects breast cancer earlier, so patients appear to survive longer from the time of diagnosis, even though overall mortality remains unchanged.

Consider two patients with the same disease.

This creates a false impression of benefit, emphasizing why mortality reduction—not survival time alone—is the correct endpoint for screening effectiveness.

A. Hawthorne bias- Occurs when participants change their behaviour because they know they are being observed. Example: workers improving productivity when being monitored.

B. Pygmalion bias- Also called observer expectancy bias. Researchers’ expectations influence participants’ outcomes.

C. Berksonian bias- A selection bias seen in hospital-based case-control studies, where hospitalized patients are not representative of the general population.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A researcher examines the relationship between per capita alcohol consumption and liver cirrhosis mortality rate across 10 countries. Identify the type of study.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ecological study

An ecological (correlational) study examines the relationship between exposure and disease at the population or group level, rather than at the individual level. It compares aggregate data (e.g., countries, states, or communities) to identify associations and generate hypotheses but cannot establish causality due to the ecological fallacy.

• The study compares per capita alcohol consumption and cirrhosis mortality rates across countries, where the unit of analysis is the population (country), making it an ecological study.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cohort study: Follows individuals over time based on exposure status.
• B. Case-control study: Begins with individual cases and controls and compares past exposures.
• C. Cross-sectional study: Measures exposure and outcome simultaneously in individuals at a single point in time.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A school-based health program teaches children about healthy eating, regular physical activity, and avoidance of smoking before they develop any lifestyle-related risk factors. This intervention represents which level of prevention?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Primordial prevention

• Primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence or development of risk factors themselves.
• Lifestyle-related risk factors for chronic diseases—such as unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, smoking, obesity, and hypertension—often develop from habits established during childhood. Therefore, educating children to adopt healthy behaviors before these risk factors appear is a classic example of primordial prevention.
• The major approach to primordial prevention is individual and mass education aimed at preventing the establishment of unhealthy lifestyles.

Why not the other options?

• A. Primary prevention: Acts before disease develops, but generally targets individuals in whom risk factors may already be present. It includes health promotion and specific protection, such as immunization.
• B. Secondary prevention: Involves early diagnosis and prompt treatment, typically through screening and case detection.
• C. Tertiary prevention: Acts after disease is established to limit disability, prevent complications, and promote rehabilitation.
• D. Primordial prevention: Prevents the development of risk factors themselves, particularly by establishing healthy behaviors early in life.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study compares IT professionals with neurological disease and healthy controls and asks about past electronic gadget use. Which bias is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Recall bias

• This is a case-control study.
• Participants are asked to remember previous exposure.
• Cases often recall exposures more completely than controls.
• This differential remembering is recall bias.
• Recall bias is a form of information bias.
• It commonly affects retrospective studies.
• Attrition bias occurs due to loss to follow-up.
• Berksonian bias is a hospital-based selection bias.
• Hawthorne effect occurs when behavior changes because participants know they are being observed.
• Recall bias can overestimate or underestimate the true association.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study finds that exercise reduces the incidence of cardiovascular disease. However, it was found that people who exercise also tend to consume a healthy diet. What does a healthy diet act in this context?
options: There is no association, it can be ignored
Diet is a mediator for reducing cardiovascular disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Confounding factor

A confounder is a variable that:

1. Is associated with the exposure (exercise)
2. Is independently associated with the outcome (CVD)
3. Is not on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome

✔ A healthy diet is associated with exercise

✔ A healthy diet independently reduces CVD risk

✔ Diet is not caused by exercise in the causal pathway being tested

This fulfils all criteria for a confounding factor.

An effect modifier:

• Alters the strength or direction of the association between exposure and outcome
• Is identified by stratified analysis, showing different effect sizes in different strata

In the question: There is no mention of stratified effects; Only co-existence of diet with exercise is described. So, effect modification is not demonstrated.

Example:

Exercise may reduce CVD more strongly in young people than elderly.

Healthy diet in this question does not modify the effect, it distorts it.

In Conclusion,

Confounding = Mixing of effects

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A town has a population of 10,000. During the past year, 60 deaths were recorded. Of these, 8 deaths were attributed to tuberculosis, 20 to cardiovascular diseases, and the remaining to other causes. What is the proportional mortality due to tuberculosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 13.3%

Proportional Mortality (PM) indicates the proportion of all deaths that are due to a specific cause. It reflects the relative contribution of a disease to total mortality and does not measure the risk of dying.

Formula:

Here:

• Deaths due to tuberculosis = 8
• Total deaths = 60

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A traveller who has passed through a yellow fever endemic zone and does not possess a Certificate of Vaccination against yellow fever, enters a yellow fever ‘receptive’ area. For how long from the date of leaving the infected area must this traveller be placed on quarantine in a mosquito-proof ward?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6 days

Yellow fever is a quarantinable viral disease transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. According to the International Health Regulations (IHR), a traveler arriving from a yellow fever endemic area without a valid Yellow Fever Vaccination Certificate may be placed under surveillance or quarantine in a mosquito-proof facility for up to 6 days from the date of leaving the infected area, corresponding to the maximum incubation period.

• Incubation period of yellow fever: 3–6 days
• Quarantine period: 6 days from the date of leaving the infected area.
• Vector: Aedes aegypti mosquito.
• Reservoir: Monkeys (jungle cycle) and humans (urban cycle).
• Prevention: Live attenuated 17D yellow fever vaccine.
• International Certificate of Vaccination becomes valid 10 days after vaccination and is valid for life.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: About two-thirds of stroke cases in a community are due to hypertension and could be prevented if hypertension were controlled. This is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Population Attributable Risk

Population Attributable Risk (PAR) estimates the proportion of disease in the entire population that is attributable to a specific risk factor. It represents the potential reduction in disease burden if the risk factor were completely eliminated, making it a valuable measure for public health planning and preventive strategies.

• The statement refers to all stroke cases in the community and indicates that two-thirds could be prevented if hypertension were controlled.
• This describes the impact of eliminating a risk factor at the population level, which is the definition of Population Attributable Risk (PAR).

Why not the other options?

• A. Relative Risk (RR): Measures the strength of association between exposure and disease in exposed versus unexposed individuals.
• B. Attributable Risk (AR): Measures the excess risk among exposed individuals attributable to the exposure.
• C. Odds Ratio (OR): Measures the association between exposure and disease, mainly in case-control studies.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: After attending a birthday party in a hostel around 50 students reported having loose stools, fever and pre-ported vomiting. This outbreak can be interpreted as what type of outbreak?
options: Both propagated and common point source
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Common point source only

A common point source outbreak occurs when a group of people is exposed to the same source over a short period, such as contaminated food served at a birthday party. Cases occur within one incubation period, producing a sharp epidemic curve.

Why not the other options?

• A. Propagated only❌: Person-to-person spread (e.g., measles, chickenpox).
• C. Common source continuous❌: Exposure occurs over days to weeks (e.g., contaminated water supply).
• D. Both propagated and common point source❌: No evidence of secondary person-to-person transmission.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are Bradford Hill's causal criteria, EXCEPT:

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are effective modalities for the prevention of spread of COVID-19 diseases except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ivermectin

COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2, which spreads mainly through respiratory droplets, aerosols and close person-to-person contact. Public health measures focus on interrupting transmission.

Prevention of COVID-19 transmission relies on non-pharmacological measures such as mask use and cough etiquette, along with vaccination to reduce infection, severity, and community spread.

Ivermectin has no proven role in preventing or treating COVID-19 based on large, well-conducted clinical trials and public health recommendations, it is primarily used to treat parasitic infections

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Among the following which is considered as water borne hepatitis virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatitis A virus

Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is transmitted via the fecal–oral route, commonly through contaminated water and food, making it a water-borne hepatitis virus. Hepatitis E virus is also primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route.

Hepatitis B, C, and D are primarily blood-borne and parenterally transmitted, not water-borne.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An infectious disease has its incubation period as 5-14 days, with its median incubation period being 10 days. The quarantine of contacts traveling to a new country should be done for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 14 days

The quarantine period is based on the maximum incubation period of the disease to ensure that all infected contacts manifest symptoms, if present.

Even though the median incubation period is 10 days, some individuals may develop disease as late as 14 days.

Therefore, quarantining contacts for 14 days is necessary to effectively prevent transmission during travel or population movement.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Arrange the following steps of a Randomised controlled trial in sequential order: 1. Manipulation 2. Statistical analysis 3. Follow-up 4. Randomisation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4-1-3-2

A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) is the gold standard experimental study design used to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions such as drugs, vaccines, or preventive measures.

The essential features of an RCT are:

• Randomization
• Manipulation (intervention)
• Control group
• Follow-up

These components ensure minimal bias and strong causal inference.

In a Randomised Controlled Trial, participants are first allocated to groups by randomisation to minimize selection bias. This is followed by manipulation, where the intervention is applied to the experimental group.

Participants are then followed up to observe outcomes, and finally statistical analysis is performed to compare results between groups.

Advantages of RCTs

Limitations

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Assertion (A): A nested case-control study can provide an accurate estimate of the relative risk. Reason (R): Cases and controls are selected from a cohort in which incidence data are already available.
options: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

A nested case-control study is conducted within an established cohort. Since the cohort is followed prospectively, incident cases are identified, and controls are selected from the same risk set. Availability of cohort incidence data allows the odds ratio to closely approximate the relative risk.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Assertion (A): Nested case-control studies can precisely estimate the relative risk. Reason (R): They use incidence data from the cohort.
options: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

A nested case-control study is a case-control study conducted within an established cohort. Because both cases and controls are selected from the same cohort with known follow-up, the study uses incidence data, allowing an accurate estimation of the relative risk (through the incidence rate ratio/hazard ratio) while being more efficient and cost-effective than analyzing the entire cohort.

Why is B correct?

• Assertion (A): Nested case-control studies can precisely estimate the relative risk. ✓
• Reason (R): They use incidence data from the parent cohort. ✓
• The reason correctly explains the assertion, because the availability of cohort follow-up and incidence information enables valid estimation of relative risk.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Best level of evidence as seen in research is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Meta-analysis

In evidence-based medicine (EBM), research studies are ranked according to the strength and reliability of evidence they provide. This ranking is known as the Hierarchy of Evidence. The higher the level, the more reliable the conclusions for clinical decision-making and public health guidelines.

Meta-analysis provides the highest level of evidence as it statistically combines results from multiple high-quality studies, usually randomized controlled trials, increasing power, precision, and reliability of conclusions.

Exam Pearls

⭐ Meta-analysis = highest level of research evidence

⭐ Systematic review often includes meta-analysis

⭐ RCT = gold standard for clinical trials

⭐ Observational studies have lower evidence

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following definition: “A high level of infection beginning early in life and affecting most of the child population, leading to a state of equilibrium such that the adult population shows evidence of the disease much less commonly than the children.” Which one of the following terms best fits this definition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Holoendemic

A holoendemic disease is one in which infection occurs at a very high level early in childhood, affecting most children in the community. As immunity develops with repeated exposure, adults are less commonly affected or have milder disease, resulting in an epidemiological equilibrium.

• Very high infection rates in children
• Early acquisition of infection
• Development of partial immunity with age
• Lower prevalence or milder disease in adults

• Example: Falciparum malaria in parts of sub-Saharan Africa.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Hyperendemic: Disease is persistently present at a high level in all age groups, without the characteristic age-related pattern seen in holoendemicity.
• C. Hypoendemic: Disease occurs at a low, stable level with relatively low transmission.
• D. Pandemic: Refers to an epidemic that spreads across multiple countries or continents, affecting a large proportion of the population.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statement: “The people should seek to preserve their traditional eating patterns and lifestyles associated with low levels of Coronary Heart Disease (CHD).” Which level of prevention is implied in this statement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primordial

Primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence of risk factors themselves by promoting healthy lifestyles and preventing the development of social, environmental, and behavioral conditions that increase disease risk. It is particularly important for non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as coronary heart disease (CHD), diabetes, and hypertension.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. High-risk approach: Targets individuals already at increased risk (e.g., smokers, hypertensive patients).
• C. Primary prevention: Prevents disease after risk factors have already developed, such as treating hypertension or promoting smoking cessation.
• D. Secondary prevention: Involves early diagnosis and prompt treatment to halt disease progression.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Data obtained from hospital records is not a representative sample of the population. What are the reasons for this? I. Mild cases and subclinical cases may be missed. II. Population served by a hospital usually cannot be defined. III. Cost of hospital care is not recorded. IV. Admission policy for cases can vary from hospital to hospital. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. I, II and IV

Hospital records are an important source of health data but are not representative of the general population. They are subject to selection bias, as only individuals who seek or require hospital care are included.

The reasons include:

• Mild and subclinical cases are often missed, since they usually do not present to hospitals.
• The population served by a hospital is often ill-defined, making it difficult to calculate population-based disease rates.
• Admission policies differ between hospitals, leading to variations in the types and severity of cases admitted.

Cost of hospital care is not a reason why hospital records are unrepresentative of the population.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During an investigation of a community outbreak of acute febrile illness (AFI), an epidemic curve is plotted with number of cases against time of onset of illness. Multiple successive peaks separated by approximately one incubation period are seen, indicating a propagated epidemic. Which disease is associated with this type of epidemic curve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Measles

A propagated epidemic results from person-to-person transmission, producing multiple successive peaks on the epidemic curve, with each peak occurring approximately one incubation period after the previous one. Measles is the classic example of a propagated epidemic because of its high infectivity and direct respiratory transmission.

• Measles spreads from one infected individual to another, leading to successive waves of new cases, which produce a propagated epidemic curve.

Why not the other options?

• B. Typhoid fever: Usually causes a common-source epidemic through contaminated food or water.
• C. Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning: Produces a point-source epidemic due to ingestion of preformed toxin.
• D. Salmonellosis: Commonly causes a common-source food-borne outbreak, not a propagated epidemic.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Given below is a table showing diagnosis of Myocardial infarction by ECG. Consider the following statements: I. Sensitivity is 90%. II. Specificity is 80%. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both I and II

The performance of a diagnostic test is assessed using sensitivity and specificity, which are calculated from a 2 × 2 contingency table. From the given table:

| | MI Present | MI Absent

| --- | ---------- | ---------

| ECG Positive | 45 (TP) | 8,000 (FP)

| ECG Negative | 5 (FN) | 32,000 (TN)

• TP (True Positive) = 45
• FN (False Negative) = 5
• FP (False Positive) = 8,000
• TN (True Negative) = 32,000

Sensitivity and specificity are the two fundamental measures used to evaluate the accuracy of a diagnostic test.

• Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) × 100 = 45 / (45 + 5) × 100 = 90%
• Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) × 100 = 32,000 / (32,000 + 8,000) × 100 = 80%

Hence, both statements are correct.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the study design shown in the figure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Case-control study

• The study begins with cases (disease) and controls (no disease).
• Investigators then look backward to assess previous exposure.
• Hence, the direction of inquiry is outcome → exposure.
• Case-control studies are useful for rare diseases.
• They are relatively quick and inexpensive.
• Measure of association is the Odds Ratio (OR).
• Incidence cannot be calculated directly.
• Multiple exposures can be evaluated.
• They are particularly prone to recall bias and selection bias.
• Cohort studies, in contrast, begin with exposure and follow participants forward.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a district, an intervention-based trial is being conducted on Neonatal sepsis. 20 PHCs were randomly chosen to follow the Standard treatment, and 20 PHCs were chosen for Community based treatment strategy. This is which type of epidemiological study design?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Clustered randomised controlled trial

A Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial (Cluster RCT) is an experimental study where groups of individuals (clusters) rather than individual participants are randomized to intervention or control arms.

Clusters can include:

• Villages
• Schools
• Hospitals
• Primary Health Centres (PHCs)

In this question:

• The unit of randomization = PHCs
• Patients within those PHCs receive the assigned strategy

In this study, entire PHCs (groups/clusters)—not individual patients—are randomly allocated to different interventions (standard treatment vs community-based strategy). When randomization is done at the group level (e.g., villages, schools, PHCs), the design is a cluster randomized controlled trial (cluster RCT).

Cluster randomization is useful when:

Quasi-experimental study: Lacks either randomization or control group; here both are mentioned. Example: Before–after intervention without random assignment.

C. Cross-sectional studies- measure exposure and outcome at a single point in time.

Example: prevalence surveys.

D. Case-control study-

• Start with disease status
• Look backwards to determine exposure

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a given population of 10,000, there were 30 cases of diabetes already present on 01/01/2025 and in the year 2025, 400 more cases developed diabetes. But 10 cases of diabetes died in the year 2025, i.e. before 31/12/2025. Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the disease situation?
options: The incidence of diabetes in the population is 42/1000.
The point prevalence of diabetes on 31/12/2025 was 43/1000.
The period prevalence of diabetes in 2025 was 43/1000.
The prevalence of diabetes in 2025 was 44/1000.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The period prevalence of diabetes in 2025 was 43/1000.

Given population = 10,000

• Existing cases on 01/01/2025 = 30
• New cases during 2025 = 400
• Total persons who had diabetes at any time during 2025 = 30 + 400 = 430

Period prevalence:

Period prevalence = (Existing cases + New cases during period) / Population × 1000

= 430 / 10,000 × 1000

= 43/1000

Therefore, C. is correct.

Why the other options are incorrect:

• A. The incidence of diabetes in the population is 42/1000: Incidence = 400 / population at risk (10,000 − 30) × 1000 ≈ 40.1/1000, not 42/1000.
• B. The point prevalence of diabetes on 31/12/2025 was 43/1000: Point prevalence on 31/12/2025 = (30 + 400 − 10) / 10,000 × 1000 = 42/1000, not 43/1000.
• D. The prevalence of diabetes in 2025 was 44/1000: Prevalence is not 44/1000.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a historical study, the death rate among heavy smokers was 224 per 1 lakh person-years while among non-smokers was 10 per 1 lakh person-years. The death rate in the general population was 74 per 1 lakh person-years. Which one among the following best represents the attributable risk of smoking for mortality in the given scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 95.5%

Attributable risk percent (AR%) is calculated as:

AR% = [(Incidence in exposed − Incidence in unexposed) / Incidence in exposed] × 100

Given:

Incidence in smokers = 224 per 1 lakh person-years

Incidence in non-smokers = 10 per 1 lakh person-years

AR% = [(224 − 10) / 224] × 100

= (214 / 224) × 100

= 95.5%

Therefore, the correct answer is C. 95.5%.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a hospital-based study, 1000 women were screened for breast cancer and those with positive findings were subsequently treated. Which level of prevention does this scenario represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Secondary

Secondary prevention involves early detection of disease through screening followed by prompt treatment to halt disease progression, reduce complications, and improve outcomes. Breast cancer screening (e.g., mammography) with subsequent treatment of detected cases is a classic example of secondary prevention.

Why not the other options?

• A. Primordial: Prevents the development of risk factors (e.g., promoting healthy lifestyle policies).
• B. Primary: Prevents the occurrence of disease before it develops (e.g., vaccination, smoking cessation).
• D. Tertiary: Focuses on limiting disability and rehabilitation after disease has been established.

| Level of Prevention | Definition | Target | Examples

| ------------------- | ---------- | ------ | --------

| Primordial | Prevents the emergence of risk factors | Healthy population | Healthy lifestyle promotion, tobacco control policies, promoting physical activity, healthy diet in children

| Primary | Prevents the occurrence of disease before it develops | Susceptible individuals | Immunization, chemoprophylaxis, smoking cessation, use of condoms, iodized salt

| Secondary | Early diagnosis and prompt treatment to halt disease progression | Early/asymptomatic disease | Mammography for breast cancer, Pap smear, BP screening, blood glucose screening, newborn screening

| Tertiary | Limits disability, complications, and restores function | Established disease | Cardiac rehabilitation after MI, physiotherapy after stroke, dialysis in CKD, diabetic foot care

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a population where the prevalence of hypertension is 30%, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3.75% will get adequate treatment

Rule of Halves in chronic diseases such as hypertension: only half of hypertensive individuals are diagnosed, half of those diagnosed receive treatment, and only half of those treated achieve adequate control. Thus, only 1/8 (12.5%) of all hypertensive individuals are adequately treated.

Calculation:

• Prevalence of hypertension = 30%
• Adequately treated = 30% × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 30% × 1/8 = 3.75%

Why not the other options?

• A. 5%: Does not follow the Rule of Halves.
• B. 7.5%: Represents 30% × 1/4, not the proportion adequately treated.
• D. 10%: Incorrect calculation; exceeds the expected proportion under the Rule of Halves.

Rule of Halves:

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study, 100 patients were contacted by phone to assess both their daily exercise habits and history of coronary artery disease. Which study design best describes this investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cross sectional study

A cross-sectional study is an observational study in which both the exposure (daily exercise habits) and the outcome (history of coronary artery disease) are assessed simultaneously at a single point in time. It provides a snapshot of the population, is primarily used to estimate disease prevalence and study associations, but cannot establish a temporal relationship or causality.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cohort study: Begins with exposed and unexposed individuals and follows them over time to compare disease incidence.
• B. Case-control study: Begins with patients with disease (cases) and without disease (controls) and looks backward to compare prior exposures.
• D. Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT): Participants are randomly assigned to intervention and control groups to evaluate the effect of a treatment or preventive measure.

| Feature | Cross-sectional Study | Case-Control Study | Cohort Study | Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT)

| ------- | --------------------- | ------------------ | ------------ | ---------------------------------

| Direction | No follow-up (snapshot) | Backward (Outcome → Exposure) | Forward (Exposure → Outcome) | Forward (Intervention → Outcome)

| Starts with | Entire population/sample | Cases and controls | Exposed and unexposed groups | Random allocation to intervention/control

| Exposure & outcome | Measured simultaneously | Past exposure assessed | Exposure assessed before disease | Investigator assigns exposure/intervention

| Measures | Prevalence | Odds Ratio (OR) | Incidence, Relative Risk (RR) | Efficacy, RR, ARR, NNT

| Best used for | Estimating disease burden, generating hypotheses | Rare diseases, diseases with long latency | Rare exposures, studying natural history | Evaluating treatments and preventive interventions

| Can establish temporality? | No | Limited | Yes | Yes

| Can establish causality? | No | Limited | Better evidence | Highest level of evidence

| Example | Survey assessing exercise habits and CAD history at one time | Compare smoking history in lung cancer patients vs controls | Follow smokers and non-smokers to compare lung cancer incidence |

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a village population, patients having diabetes and hypertension are enumerated. Then their family members are screening for diabetes and hypertension. This is a type of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Selective screening

Screening is the process of identifying disease in apparently healthy individuals so that early treatment can be initiated.

Types:

Selective screening targets individuals or groups with a higher probability of disease rather than the entire population.

Screening family members of known diabetic and hypertensive patients focuses on those with shared genetic and environmental risk factors, making it selective rather than mass screening.

A: Opportunistic screening = done when patient visits health facility for another reason is screened for additional diseases.

C: Multiphasic screening = multiple tests in one sitting (not defined by risk group)

D : Mass screening = entire population, not restricted to families, regardless of risks.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a village with 100 children, 10 had developed measles in the previous year. In the current year, 20 children developed measles for the first time. What is the incidence rate of measles for the current year?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 22.2%

Incidence rate includes only new cases among the population at risk during a specified period.

At the start of the current year, 10 children already had measles, so they are not at risk.

Population at risk = 100 − 10 = 90.

New cases = 20

Incidence = (20 ÷ 90) × 100 = 22.2%

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In India, 30% of all deaths are due to Coronary Heart Disease (CHD). Which measure of disease burden is most appropriate to describe this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proportional mortality rate

Proportional Mortality Rate (PMR) is the proportion of all deaths in a population attributable to a specific cause during a given period. It reflects the relative contribution of a disease to total mortality, not the risk of dying from that disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. Case fatality rate: Measures the proportion of diagnosed cases that die from a disease; indicates disease severity.
• C. Crude death rate: Total deaths per 1,000 population per year, irrespective of cause.
• D. Specific death rate: Death rate in a specific population group (e.g., age- or sex-specific) or due to a specific cause, expressed per population at risk.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the conduct of a randomized controlled trial (RCT), participants are enrolled and followed using a predefined methodological sequence. Which of the following represents the correct chronological order of key steps in an RCT?
options: Data analysis → Blinding → Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation
Blinding → Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation → Data analysis
Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation → Blinding → Data analysis
Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Blinding → Random allocation → Data analysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation → Blinding → Data analysis

A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) begins with defining inclusion and exclusion criteria to select an appropriate study population.

Eligible participants are then randomized into intervention and control groups, followed by blinding to reduce bias.

Finally, outcomes are assessed and subjected to statistical analysis, completing the trial process.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the history of public health, as a part of modern medicine, the following four distinct phases can be demarcated: 1. Health for All phase 2. Health promotional phase 3. Disease control phase 4. Social engineering phase Which one of the following represents the correct sequence of the phases in chronological order (from the oldest to the newest)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 → 2 → 4 → 1

The historical evolution of public health can be broadly divided into four phases:

1. Disease control phase — Oldest

• Focused primarily on controlling communicable diseases through sanitation, vaccination, isolation and other disease-specific measures.

2. Health promotional phase

• Shifted emphasis toward health education, lifestyle modification and promotion of healthy behaviours.

3. Social engineering phase

• Recognized that health is strongly influenced by social, economic, environmental and political determinants.

4. Health for All phase — Newest

• Emphasized equity, primary health care and universal access to essential health services, particularly following the Alma-Ata Declaration.

Therefore:

Disease control → Health promotional → Social engineering → Health for All

3 → 2 → 4 → 1 → C.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In which one of the following study designs, the unit of study involves populations rather than individuals?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ecological studies

An ecological (correlational) study is an observational study in which the unit of analysis is a population or group rather than an individual. It examines the relationship between exposure and disease using aggregate (group-level) data.

• A. Ecological studies ✓

• Unit of study: Populations or groups
• Example: Correlating per capita salt intake with stroke mortality across different countries.

• B. Cross-sectional studies ✗

• Unit of study is the individual.
• Measures exposure and outcome simultaneously.

• C. Case-control studies ✗

• Unit of study is the individual.
• Compares cases and controls to identify past exposures.

• D. Cohort studies ✗

• Unit of study is the individual.
• Follows exposed and unexposed individuals over time to measure disease occurrence.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: John Snow’s discovery that cholera is a waterborne disease was the outcome of which type of study?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Natural experiment

John Snow’s investigation of the 1854 London cholera outbreak is a classic example of a natural experiment. He compared cholera cases among populations supplied by different water companies, where the exposure (contaminated vs. clean water) occurred naturally rather than being assigned by the investigator. This study established that cholera is a waterborne disease and laid the foundation of modern epidemiology.

• In a natural experiment, the investigator does not allocate the exposure; instead, naturally occurring differences in exposure are studied.
• He also demonstrated the source of infection by linking cases to the Broad Street water pump, leading to removal of its handle and a decline in cases.

Why not the other options?

• A. Uncontrolled trial: There was no intervention without a comparison group.
• C. Risk factor trial: Risk factor trials are experimental studies evaluating modification of risk factors and are not applicable here.
• D. Trial of aetiological agent: It is unethical to deliberately expose individuals to a disease-causing agent.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Malaria diagnosis under field settings is best done by using?
options: Rapid diagnostic test (HRP Type 2 Pf Antigen)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rapid diagnostic test (HRP Type 2 Pf Antigen)

In field conditions, rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are preferred for malaria detection because they are quick, simple, and do not require laboratory infrastructure.

• These tests commonly detect Histidine-Rich Protein 2 (HRP2), which is specific for Plasmodium falciparum.
• RDTs are based on immunochromatographic techniques and provide results within minutes, making them ideal for peripheral or resource-limited settings.

Key Antigens Detected in RDTs:

• HRP2 → specific for P. falciparum
• pLDH (parasite lactate dehydrogenase) → pan-malarial antigen (detects multiple species)

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Thick smear: Highly sensitive but requires microscopy, trained personnel, and lab setup → not ideal for field use.
• Thin smear: Useful for species identification and parasite quantification, but also requires lab facilities.
• Quantitative buffy coat (QBC): Sensitive technique but needs special equipment (centrifuge + fluorescent microscope) → impractical in field settings.

Field diagnosis prioritizes:

• Speed
• Minimal infrastructure
• Ease of use

→ Hence, antigen-based rapid tests (HRP2) are the most practical choice.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Many patients with unexplained rash and fever were reported from a village close to the Primary Health Centre (PHC). What is the first step in initiating the investigation of such an epidemic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Verification of diagnosis

The first step in investigating a suspected epidemic (outbreak) is to verify the diagnosis. This involves confirming that the reported cases are correctly diagnosed through clinical evaluation and appropriate laboratory investigations. Verification helps exclude diagnostic errors, laboratory mistakes, or misclassification before initiating a full-scale outbreak investigation. Verification includes:

• Reviewing clinical findings
• Examining laboratory reports
• Consulting clinicians and microbiologists
• Excluding laboratory or reporting errors

Why not the other options?

• A. Rapid search for all cases: This is done after the diagnosis has been verified and the outbreak has been confirmed.
• C. Confirm existence of epidemic: An epidemic can be confirmed only after ensuring that the diagnosis is correct.
• D. Defining the population at risk: This is a later step used to calculate attack rates and identify risk factors.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Numerous youngsters from a specific community arrived at a medical facility and were diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It was assumed that it is due to the presence of cytotoxic waste in the water of that community. If a case-control investigation were to be conducted to find the potential association between the chemical waste and ALL, what would serve as the control group?
options: Children from the area exposed, but unaffected with the disease
Children from the area not exposed and affected with the disease
Children coming to the OPD who do not have the disease
All children with ALL irrespective of exposure status
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Children coming to the OPD who do not have the disease

In a case–control study, controls must be free of the disease and should represent the population from which the cases arose, irrespective of exposure status.

Selecting children attending the OPD without ALL fulfills this requirement, as they reflect the background exposure distribution of the source population.

Children attending the OPD without the disease can serve as hospital controls.

Hospital controls are commonly used in case–control studies because:

·         They come from the same healthcare setting

·         They are accessible and easier to recruit

·         They do not have the disease being studied

Thus they can be compared with cases to evaluate previous exposure to contaminated water.

Controls should not be chosen based on exposure or disease presence, and cases (ALL patients) can never serve as controls, making option C correct.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Research is being conducted to find the association between aniline dye exposure and bladder cancer in workers who have worked in the industry for >20 years. Two groups were formed: one directly involved with dye handling and the other group consisting of office clerks not directly exposed to the dye. Years of occupation were noted from records. Then Bladder cancer cases were identified from both the groups in the current time. What type of study is being performed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retrospective cohort study

The study begins by classifying participants based on past exposure to aniline dye using existing records, and then determines the occurrence of bladder cancer at the present time.

Because both exposure and follow-up period lie in the past, with outcomes ascertained later, this design is a retrospective cohort study.

Unlike case–control studies, participants are selected by exposure status, and no intervention is introduced, distinguishing it from experimental designs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: STDs are transmitted by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Direct contact

Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs)/Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are primarily transmitted through direct sexual contact with an infected individual. Transmission occurs through vaginal, anal, or oral sexual intercourse, as well as exposure to infected genital secretions or lesions.

• A. Direct contact ✓: Correct. The principal mode of transmission of STDs is direct sexual contact.
• B. Droplet infection ✗: Used for infections such as influenza, measles, and pertussis.
• C. Contact with soil ✗: Seen in diseases like tetanus and certain helminthic infections.
• D. Vector borne ✗: Seen in diseases such as malaria, dengue, and filariasis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Submerged portion of iceberg shows which disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mild cases of Influenza

The iceberg phenomenon illustrates that the clinically apparent cases of a disease represent only a small visible portion, while a much larger submerged portion consists of subclinical, mild, or inapparent cases.

• Submerged portion includes:

• Subclinical infections
• Mild or atypical cases
• Undiagnosed cases
• Carriers (where applicable)

Measles, tetanus, rabies (+/- rubella) are exceptions to this theory and do not show the submerged cases and all cases are clinically apparent.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The changes that the malarial parasite undergoes in the mosquito represent which one of the following types of biological transmission?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cyclopropagative

In malaria, the parasite undergoes both:

• Development → sexual and developmental changes occur inside the mosquito.
• No multiplication of the parasite in the mosquito vector in the sense relevant to this classification? Actually, the parasite undergoes multiplication as well as development, making malaria transmission cyclopropagative.

Therefore, the correct answer is C. Cyclopropagative.

Exam Pearl:

Types of Transmission in Vectors

1. Propagative

• Example: Plague bacilli in rat fleas, YF in Aedes

2. Cyclo-propagative

• Example: Malarial parasites in Anopheles

3. Cyclo-developmental

• Example: Microfilaria in Culex

4. Transovarial

• Example: Rickettsia rickettsii in ticks, Mite in scrub typhus

5. Transstadial

• Example: Borrelia burgdorferi, Indian tick typhus

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The following table shows the mortality figures among hazardous industry workers. What is the Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR) for the hazardous industry workers (as compared to national population)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 120

Standardized Mortality Ratio (SMR) is a measure obtained by indirect standardization. It compares the observed number of deaths in the study population with the expected number of deaths if the study population had the same age-specific mortality rates as the standard population.

SMR = (Observed deaths / Expected deaths) × 100

• Total expected deaths = 6 + 7 + 12 = 25
• Total observed deaths = 8 + 9 + 13 = 30

SMR = (30 / 25) × 100 = 120

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The maximum tolerable dose for a new drug is assessed in which phase of Clinical trial?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phase 1

Phase I clinical trials are the first studies conducted in humans, primarily aimed at assessing safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and dose range of a new drug.

They help determine the maximum tolerated dose and appropriate dosage schedules, usually in a small number of healthy volunteers.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The parameter which provides an estimate of the amount by which the disease under study can be reduced in a population, if the suspected factor is eliminated from that population, is called:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Population attributable risk

Population attributable risk (PAR) estimates the amount of disease occurrence in the entire population that could be prevented if the suspected risk factor were completely eliminated.

• A. Relative risk: Measures the risk of disease in exposed compared with unexposed.
• B. Attributable risk: Measures the excess risk among the exposed population due to the exposure.
• C. Population attributable risk — Correct: Estimates the disease burden in the total population attributable to the exposure.
• D. Risk difference: Difference in risk between exposed and unexposed; essentially the same concept as attributable risk in many contexts.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The population of an area is 90,000. On January 1, there were 30 existing TB cases. During the year, 15 new cases occurred with no deaths or migration. Calculate the period prevalence per 1,000 population.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 0.5

• Period prevalence includes existing + new cases during the specified period.
• Total TB cases = 30 + 15 = 45.
• Population = 90,000.
• Formula:

• Existing cases contribute to prevalence.
• Newly diagnosed cases during the period are also included.
• Since there were no deaths or migration, all 45 cases remain.
• Prevalence measures disease burden, not risk.
• Incidence would include only the 15 new cases.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The time gap between entry of organism in human body and its maximal infectivity is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Generation time

Generation time is defined as the interval between the entry of an infectious agent into the human body and the point at which the host reaches maximum infectivity.

he question asks for the interval between infection and the time when the host becomes most infectious to others.

Key phrase in the question:

“maximal infectivity”

This is a defining characteristic of generation time.

It is a key concept in understanding the speed of disease transmission and epidemic potential. This differs from the incubation period, which measures time to symptom onset, and the serial interval, which refers to time between successive cases.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The typical lifespan for a Japanese woman is 87 years. Due to recent progress in cervical cancer testing, her life expectancy has risen by 15 years. With a healthcare utility value of 0.8, what can be determined based on these provided parameters?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. QALY

Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALY) combine quantity of life gained with quality of life, expressed as a utility value.

Here, an increase of 15 life years with a utility of 0.8 directly fits the QALY framework (QALY = life years × utility).

DALY measures health loss, while HALE and DFLE are population-level expectancy measures, not used for individual intervention benefit.

| Indicator | Measures

| --------- | --------

| QALY | Benefit of health intervention

| DALY | Burden of disease

| HALE | Healthy life expectancy

| DFLE | Life expectancy without disability

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) primarily contributes to which level of prevention?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary

The Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) is a community-level committee under the National Health Mission (NHM) that focuses on health promotion, disease prevention, sanitation, nutrition, and community participation. Its activities are aimed at preventing disease before it occurs, making it an example of primary prevention.

VHSNC activities include:

• Health education
• Promotion of sanitation and hygiene
• Nutrition awareness
• Safe drinking water
• Immunization support
• Maternal and child health promotion

These measures are components of primary prevention.

Why not the other options?

• A. Primordial: Prevents the emergence of risk factors through broad policy and environmental measures.
• C. Secondary: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment (e.g., screening).
• D. Tertiary: Disability limitation and rehabilitation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: To study the effect of Vitamin C consumption on the occurrence of Respiratory disease, arrange the steps of a case-control study in sequence. 1 – Measurement of exposure. 2 – Matching. 3 – Analysis and interpretation. 4 – Selection of cases and controls.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4213

A case–control study begins with selection of cases and appropriate controls based on disease status. This design is especially useful for:

• Rare diseases
• Diseases with long latency periods

One classic example is the Doll and Hill Study, which demonstrated the association between smoking and lung cancer.

This is followed by matching to control for confounding variables, then measurement of past exposure to the risk factor.

Finally, analysis and interpretation are performed, commonly using odds ratio to assess the association.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the International Health Regulations which of the following diseases are notifiable by the National Health Authority to the World Health Organization? 1. Cholera 2. Plague 3. Klebsiella pneumonia 4. Yellow fever Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

Under the International Health Regulations (IHR), countries are required to notify the World Health Organization (WHO) of diseases and public health events that may constitute a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC).

Among the options given:

• 1. Cholera ✓: A notifiable disease under the classical IHR framework and an event requiring international reporting when appropriate.
• 2. Plague ✓: A notifiable disease because of its potential for rapid international spread.
• 3. Klebsiella pneumonia ✗: Not an internationally notifiable disease under the IHR.
• 4. Yellow fever ✓: A notifiable disease due to its epidemic potential and international public health importance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the national program for the non-communicable disease implemented in rural areas, which of the following is not included in the program?
options: Direct oral inspection for oral cancer
Mammography for screening at primary level
Start screening beyond 30 years of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mammography for screening at primary level

Under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS), population-based screening is conducted at the primary care level.

Screening methods include direct oral visual inspection for oral cancer, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) for cervical cancer, and clinical breast examination.

Mammography is not recommended at the primary level due to cost, infrastructure requirements, and feasibility; it is reserved for higher centres when indicated.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term used to describe a study that is longitudinal, observational, and includes the analysis of variables to determine associations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort study

A cohort study is an observational and longitudinal study design in which groups defined by exposure status are followed forward in time to assess the occurrence of outcomes. It is called longitudinal because:

• Participants are followed over a period of time
• Outcomes develop after the exposure is assessed

It helps establish temporal relationship between exposure and outcome. It allows estimation of incidence, relative risk, and temporal relationships between exposure and disease.

TYPES OF COHORT STUDIES

| Descriptor | What it rules in/out | Cohort study

| ---------- | -------------------- | ------------

| Longitudinal | Follows subjects over time (rules out cross-sectional) | ✔ subjects followed forward from exposure → outcome

| Observational | No intervention by investigator (rules out RCT/experimental) | ✔ exposure is naturally occurring, not assigned

| Analysis of variables to determine associations | Analytical, not merely descriptive | ✔ measures association (RR, incidence) between exposure and outcome

In contrast, case–control studies are retrospective, they calculate odds ratio, not relative risk. Ecological studies analyse group-level data, and RCTs are interventional.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term used to describe the period between the entry of an organism into the human body and the point of its maximum infectivity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Generation time

Generation time is defined as the interval between the entry of an infectious agent into the host and the point at which the host reaches maximum infectivity.

It reflects the speed with which an infection can spread in a population and is especially important in epidemic modeling.

Generation time helps in:

In contrast, the incubation period measures time to symptom onset, while the serial interval refers to time between successive cases.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are criteria for cancer screening? I. Screening test should be sensitive II. Screening test should be acceptable to the screened population III. The disease should be an uncommon one for screening to be effective IV. Disease should be recognisable at an early stage Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

A screening test is used to identify apparently healthy individuals who are likely to have a disease or are at increased risk, allowing early diagnosis and treatment before symptoms develop. An ideal screening program should fulfill the Wilson and Jungner criteria.

The following are essential criteria for an effective cancer screening program:

• I. Screening test should be sensitive: A good screening test should detect most cases (high sensitivity) while minimizing false positives (adequate specificity).
• II. Screening test should be acceptable to the screened population: The test should be safe, simple, affordable, minimally invasive, and acceptable to ensure good participation.
• IV. Disease should be recognizable at an early stage: There should be a detectable preclinical or early stage during which treatment improves outcomes.

Why is III incorrect?

• III. The disease should be an uncommon one for screening to be effective: This is incorrect. Screening is most beneficial for common diseases with a significant public health burden. Screening for very rare diseases is generally not cost-effective.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following factors will lead to an increase in the prevalence of a disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Longer duration of disease

The prevalence of a disease increases with the longer duration of the disease, as more individuals remain affected over time. Prevalence refers to the proportion of individuals in a population who have a specific disease at a given point in time. It is influenced by both the incidence (the rate of new cases) and the duration of the disease. When a disease has a longer duration, individuals remain affected by the disease for a longer period, thereby increasing the prevalence. This can occur in chronic conditions where treatment prolongs life without curing the disease or when there is a delay in effective treatment.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
