questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about the management of HIV patient with multiple dog bites?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rabies vaccine + immunoglobuin+ wound management

In the given scenario, an HIV patient with multiple dog bites falls under Category 3 for rabies vaccination and should receive rabies vaccine, immunoglobulin, and proper wound care.

Rabies is a fatal viral disease transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal, primarily dogs. Rabies vaccination is the most effective way to prevent the disease after exposure.

The post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen includes thorough wound cleaning, administration of the rabies vaccine, and in severe cases (Category 3 exposure), rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) for immediate virus neutralization. The rabies vaccine is administered in a series of intramuscular or intradermal doses, following schedules like the Essen regimen (0, 3, 7, 14, and 28 days) or the Zagreb regimen (0, 7, and 21 days). Immediate treatment is crucial, as rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear.

In addition to post-exposure vaccination, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is recommended for individuals at high risk, such as veterinarians, animal handlers, and travellers to rabies-endemic regions. The PrEP schedule consists of two doses on days 0 and 7, with an optional booster if needed. Mass vaccination of dogs and public awareness programs are essential for rabies prevention and control. Since human rabies cases are still reported in many countries, widespread vaccination efforts play a critical role in achieving the WHO goal of eliminating human rabies deaths by 2030.

Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted).

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):

* Passive immunization

* Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine

* Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight

* Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.

* Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

* RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.

* The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.

* RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

* Multiple bites

* Deep wounds

* Bites to head, neck, and hands

* Patients with severe immunodeficiency

* Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal

* Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

* High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.

* Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult

* Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year

* Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3.

* Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm

* Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.

* Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.

For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable:

* Proper wound management should be done.

* There is no need for the administration of RIG.

* One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3.

Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months.

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

* Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency

* Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a food adulteration disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fluorosis

Fluorosis is not classified as a disease caused by food adulteration.

Fluorosis occurs when drinking water contains excess amounts of fluorine, in the range of 3-5mg/L. It is endemic in parts of India- Andhra Pradesh (Nellore, Prakasam), Telangana(Nalgonda), Punjab, Haryana, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu.

Symptoms correspond to levels of fluoride intake:

* Dental fluorosis: (1.5mg/L).

* Skeletal fluorosis: (3-6mg/L).

* Crippling fluorosis: (>10mg/L)

Genu valgum and osteoporosis of the lower limb are seen in a newer form of fluorosis in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. It is seen in people consuming jawar (sorghum), as it promotes greater retention of ingested fluoride.

The given images show dental fluorosis and skeletal fluorosis (interosseous-membrane-calcification), respectively:

Other options:

Option A: Neurolathyrism is a neurological disorder caused by excessive consumption of Lathyrus sativus (grass pea), leading to spastic paralysis of the lower limbs. It results from the neurotoxin β-ODAP, primarily affecting populations dependent on the legume during famine.

Option B: Epidemic dropsy is a toxic disease caused by consuming adulterated mustard oil contaminated with Argemone mexicana seeds. It leads to symptoms like oedema, gastrointestinal issues, and cardiovascular complications.

Option D: Aflatoxicosis is a toxic condition caused by ingesting food contaminated with aflatoxins, which are produced by Aspergillus fungi in stored grains and nuts. It can lead to acute liver damage, jaundice, and an increased risk of liver cancer.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Varicella

Varicella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnant women as it is a live vaccine.

Live attenuated vaccines are prepared from organisms that have lost their capacity to induce full-blown disease but retain their immunogenicity and are contraindicated in pregnancy unless the risk of infection exceeds the risk of harm to the fetus.

Varicella, Mumps, BCG, Measles and Rubella vaccines are examples of live attenuated vaccines.

The live attenuated varicella virus vaccine is currently recommended for children between 12 to 18 months of age who have not had chickenpox. Following vaccination, salicylates should be avoided for 6 weeks to prevent Reye's syndrome.

Varicella vaccine is contraindicated in:

* Pregnant women

* Immunocompromised patients

* Patients allergic to neomycin

questions.text: 6x6x6 strategy under Anemia Mukt Bharat includes all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coordination/Ministries

Anemia Mukt Bharat scheme implements 6 x 6x 6 strategy which focuses on six target beneficiary groups, through six interventions and six institutional mechanisms to achieve their target by 2022.

The Anemia Mukt Bharat scheme is an initiative that aims to strengthen the existing mechanisms and foster newer strategies for tackling anemia.

Interventions include:

* Prophylactic iron and folic acid supplementation.

* Deworming.

* Intensified year-round Behaviour Change Communication Campaign (Solid Body, Smart Mind) including ensuring delayed cord clamping in newborns.

* Testing of anemia using digital methods and point-of-care treatment.

* Mandatory provision of Iron and Folic Acid fortified foods in government-funded health programs.

* Addressing non-nutritional causes of anemia in endemic pockets, with a special focus on malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis.

IFA tablet distribution under Anemia Mukt Bharat:

* Lactating mothers of 0 to 6-month-old children are given a daily dose of red color IFA tablet containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid.

* Weekly doses of red color IFA tablets containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid are given to women of reproductive age (non-pregnant, non-lactating), between 20-49 years of age.

* Children between 5-9 years of age are given pink color sugar-coated tablets containing 45 mg of elemental iron and 400 mcg of folic acid tablets once a week.

* Blue color tablets containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid can be given to school-going adolescent girls and boys of 10-19 years and out-of-school adolescent girls of age 10-19 years.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presented with complaints of bleeding gums. Blood investigations showed iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies do you expect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

Dietary deficiency of vitamin C can lead to scurvy which can manifest as microcytic anemia, defective collagen synthesis, and bleeding manifestations.

Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin. It is mainly required for the hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues of collagen reactions. It also maintains vitamin E and many metal cofactors (eg. copper) in a reduced state. It also facilitates the absorption of iron by reducing it from a ferric to a ferrous state.

Hence, vitamin C deficiency leads to defective collagen synthesis, fragile blood vessels, and iron deficiency anemia. Other clinical features of scurvy include spongy gums, loose teeth, swollen joints, subcutaneous hemorrhage, and bone fractures.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male presents with 2 weeks of cough, fever and night sweats. Investigations reveal a CD4 count of 100 /μL. Which of the following infections is most likely to be seen in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mycobacterium avium complex

The clinical vignette suggests opportunistic infection in HIV patients. The most common opportunistic infection when CD4 counts falls below 100 is disseminated mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infections

Mycobacterium avium complex, or Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex, is a group of slow-growing, nonchromogenic non-tuberculous mycobacteria. The infections occur in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed patients. It is the most frequent organism affecting HIV and immunosuppressed patients, although about 40% of pulmonary infections occur in immunocompetent patients. Cervical lymphadenitis is the most common presentation in young children of age <5 years. Other manifestations include skin, and soft tissue infections, musculoskeletal infections, and disseminated disease

Treatment with either clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol is a preferred initial therapy along with starting anti-retroviral therapy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A newly diagnosed HIV patient presented with fever, cough, and hemoptysis. What is the investigation of choice to test for TB in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CBNAAT

As per RNTCP guidelines, CBNAAT is the preferred diagnostic technique for testing TB in PLHIV (people living with HIV). Smear microscopy has poor sensitivity in detecting TB in PLHIV due to fewer organisms in sputum, and hence is not preferred.

Tuberculosis is the most common opportunistic infection in people living with HIV AIDS. The combined treatment of both TB and HIV has found to have profound impact on mortality. The main stay of treatment is to start ATT first and then start ART as soon as ATT is tolerated (between 2 weeks and 2 months) by the patient. This is done in order to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).

Patients with HIV-related TB may experience a temporary paradoxical exacerbation of symptoms and radiographic manifestations of TB after starting ATT. This occurs as a result of immune reconstitution due to simultaneous administration of ART and ATT.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the graph given below
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Propagated epidemic

The graph shows a propagated epidemic.

A propagated epidemic is one in which there is a rise and fall in the number of cases multiple times with a gradual fall in cases overall. It occurs in infectious diseases where there is person-to-person transmission. Peaks repeat when there is a spread of infection to a different set of susceptible individuals. It continues till there are no more susceptible individuals or the chances of exposure to the disease or vector come down. It is common in communities where there are large aggregates of susceptible populations or there is a continuous supply of suseptible population by birth or immigration.

Pearl PF0959: Epidemics and its Types

Epidemics and its Types

An epidemic is an occurrence in a community or region of cases of an illness that is clearly in excess of normal expectancy.

Types

Common source epidemics

* Single exposure or 'point source' epidemics

* Multiple or continuous exposure epidemics

Propagated epidemics

* Person to person

* Arthropod vector

* Animal reservoir

Slow or modern epidemics

* Non-communicable diseases

questions.text: In a study about the age of a small population, the highest value 36 was mistakenly recorded as 63. What will happen to the mean and median of the data?
options: Median will increase, mean will remain the same
Mean will increase, median will remain the same
Both mean and median will increase
Neither mean nor median will increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mean will increase, median will remain the same

When the highest recorded value is replaced by a bigger value, mean will increase while median will be unaffected.

Median

* The median is the central element in a distribution when all the elements are arranged in order.

* In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value.

* In a distribution that has an even number of elements, the median is the average of the middle values, i.e., the arithmetic mean of the two middle values.

* The median is not sensitive to extreme values, i.e., outliers and thus it is preferred measure of location for very skewed distributions.

* The drawback of the median is that it doesn’t respond to the actual values of the elements but only to the number of values above or below

* The median is the same as the 50th centile.

* It is sometimes symbolized by Mdn.

* The median can be arrived at in ordinal, interval and ratio data scales.

Pearl PF1749: The Mean (Arithmetic) in Biostatistics

* The mean is also called the average or arithmetic mean.

* It is the sum of all elements in the distribution divided by the number of all the elements in it.

* It is usually denoted by μ in a population and by x̄ (x-bar) in a sample.

* The formula for sample mean is given as:

where the sigma sign denotes summation and n is the total number of elements.

* The arithmetic mean responds to the exact value of every element in the distribution.

* This makes it over-sensitive to extreme values, i.e., outliers thus making it an inappropriate measure for skewed distributions.

* The advantage of the arithmetic mean is that if repeated samples are taken from the same populations, they will have very similar means, i.e., the measure of central tendency that best resists the influence of fluctuation between samples is the mean.

* The mean can be calculated only on quantitative data on an interval or a ratio scale.

questions.text: The number of births per 1,000 women in the reproductive age group is called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. General fertility rate

Number of live births per 1000 women in the reproductive age group (15 - 49 years) in a given year is called the general fertility rate

* GFR = Number of live births in an area in a year x 1000/Mid-year population of women in reproductive age in the same area in the same year.

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

Pearl PF1746: Fertility Indicators

Crude birth rate

* It is the simplest measure of fertility although its usage is unsatisfactory

* India, as per SRS bulletin 2018, had a birth rate of 20.0 per 1000 population

General Fertility Rate

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

Age-specific fertility rates is a more precise measure of fertility and is also a sensitive indicator of family planning achievement.

Total Fertility Rate

* It is the sum of all age-specific fertility rates multiplied by 5

* This measure gives the approximate magnitude of completed family size

Gross Reproductive Rate is the average number of girls that would be born to a woman if she experiences the current fertility pattern throughout her reproductive span, assuming no mortality.

Net Reproduction Rate

* It is a demographic indicator

* NRR of 1 is equivalent to approximately the 2 child norm

* If the NRR is less than 1, then the reproductive performance of the population is said to be inadequate

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A gym owner noticed that people who come to the gym also drink iced tea. He concluded that drinking iced tea is the sole reason to lose weight. What is this relationship called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spurious

In the gym owner's case, concluding that iced tea alone causes weight loss is a spurious relationship because it ignores other key factors like exercise and overall diet.

A spurious relationship is when two variables appear to be connected but are actually linked by another factor or are coincidental. In this scenario, the gym owner observed that gym-goers also drink iced tea and concluded that iced tea is the sole cause of weight loss. However, this conclusion is just coincidental because it ignores other important factors, such as exercise, diet, and lifestyle changes, which likely contribute to weight loss.

An association can be broadly grouped under three headings:

* Spurious association

* Indirect association

* Direct (causal) association: One-to-one causal association and Multifactorial causation

Option B: Direct (causal) association: Two variables are stated to be causally related (AB) if a change in A is followed by a change in B. When factor A is present, disease B must result. Measles is one such disease in which such a relation exists.

Option C: Indirect association: The indirect association is an association between a variable and disease due to the presence of another factor, known or unknown, that is also known as the "confounding" variable. For example, endemic goitre is generally found in high altitudes, thereby showing an association between altitude and endemic goitre. But, endemic goitre is not due to altitude but due to an environmental deficiency of iodine. Thus, a common factor (i.e., iodine deficiency) can result in an apparent association between two variables, when no association exists.

Option D: Multifactorial causation is seen in non-communicable diseases or conditions (e.g., Coronary heart disease) where the etiology is multifactorial.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A total of 4050 births were recorded over 1 year in a given population. Among these, 50 were stillbirths, 50 died in the 1st week of life and 150 died within 8–28 days of life. What is the neonatal mortality rate in this population?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 50

The neonatal mortality rate (NMR) of the given population is 50 per 1000 live births.

Neonatal mortality rate = No. of deaths of neonates < 28 days within a year x 1000 / Total live births in the same year

* No. of deaths of neonates < 28 days = (50+150)= 200

* Total live births = (Total births - stillbirths)= 4050-50= 4000

* NMR = (200 x 1000) / 4000 = 50

Pearl PF0989: Neonatal Mortality Rate

* Neonatal deaths are those that occur during the neonatal period, commencing at birth and ending at 28 completed days after birth.

* NMR = Number of deaths of children under 28 days of age in a year x 1000/Total live births in the same year

* Main causes of neonatal death are birth asphyxia (leading cause), preterm complications, intrapartum related complications, sepsis, pneumonia, congenital anomalies, tetanus, diarrhea, etc.

* India’s NMR  is about 25 per 1000 live births.

questions.text: A woman arrived at the hospital with edema, visual disturbances, and heart failure after consuming a food item purchased from a seller who has now been arrested for food adulteration. Which of the following is the most likely food adulterant used? Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sanguinarine

The clinical presentation of edema, visual disturbances, and heart failure after consuming a food item purchased from a seller who has now been arrested for food adulteration is suggestive of epidemic dropsy. Sanguinarine is the toxic compound responsible for this.

Sanguinarine causes Epidemic Dropsy.

* Contamination of mustard oil with argemone oil.

* Toxic compound: Sanguinarine

Mechanism of action : Sanguinarine interfers with the oxidation of pyruvic acid which in turn accumulates in the blood and causes symptoms.

Clinical presentation: The patient presents with sudden onset, non-inflammatory swelling of bilateral legs which is often associated with diarrhoea. Some patients can develop glaucoma. Dyspnea, cardiac failure and death can occur in later stages.

Tests to detect argemone oil:

* Nitric acid test

* Paper chromatography: most sensitive(can detect very low concentration of argemone oil)

Other options:

Option A: Aflatoxins are produced by certain fungi, such as Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, are the most potent hepatotoxins. These fungi can contaminate food grains such as groundnut, maize, parboiled rice, sorghum, wheat, and tapioca. It is mainly due to improper storage. It can be prevented by proper storage after drying. Moisture content should be kept below 10%. They do not cause the symptoms described in the question.

Option C: Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals and Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA) is the toxic compound causing this disease. Gradual spastic paralysis of lower limbs is associated with the consumption of Khesari dal/Lathyrus sativus leading to neurolathyrism.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Calculate the dependency ratio in this family. Mr J, age 68 years, Mrs J age 59, their son’s age 30 years, his wife’s age is 27 years and grandson is 5 years old.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 66.6%

The dependency ratio for this family will be 66.6%.

The dependent population includes children Population under 15 years and above 65 years are part of the numerator used to calculate the total dependency ratio. This is because this population is considered the dependent population.

Here,

Family members under 15 years = 1

Family members above 65 years = 1

Total population under 15 years and above 65 years = 1+1 = 2 (Numerator)

Total population in 15-65 years group = 3

Total dependency ratio = 2/3 x 100 = 66.6%

The total dependency ratio is the ratio of the combined dependent population to those in the age group of 15–65 years. It is also called the societal dependency ratio. It can also be divided into the young-age and old-age dependency ratios.

Note: As of mid-year 2020, the dependency ratio of India is 48.7%.

Correct answer: D. > 10 mg/L

Crippling fluorosis is seen at fluoride intake >10 mg/L.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Morbidity of a disease is on the rise. Which of the following statements is correct with respect to this?
options: Incidence will increase and prevalence will decrease
Incidence and prevalence are not related to it
Incidence will decrease and prevalence will increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Incidence and prevalence will increase

The incidence and prevalence will increase when the morbidity increases.

Morbidity refers to any deviation, whether subjective or objective, from a state of physical well-being. It encompasses conditions such as sickness, illness, and disability. Morbidity is typically measured by morbidity rates or ratios, which include frequency, duration, and severity. Disease frequency is indicated by incidence and prevalence rates.

Incidence refers to the number of new cases of a disease that occur in a population during a specific time period, while prevalence represents the total number of cases, both new and existing, in a population at a given time. Additionally, the average duration of illness, represented by the disability rate, and the severity of illnesses, indicated by the case fatality rate, are also used as measures.

As morbidity increases in a population, both incidence and prevalence rates tend to rise. This is because a higher morbidity indicates a greater number of people experiencing illness (increased incidence) and a larger number of existing cases (increased prevalence). The increased duration of illness (disability days) and the severity of conditions also contribute to the overall morbidity burden.

Pearl PF0231: Mortality and morbidity indicators in epidemiology

Crude death rate = ( Number of deaths during the year/Mid year population ) x 1000

Age specific death rate = ( Number of deaths in specific age groups/Mid year population of that age group ) x 1000

Sex specific death rate = ( Number of deaths per year of that sex/Mid year population of that sex ) x 1000

Case fatality rate = ( Total number of deaths due to a particular disease/Total number of cases due to same disease ) x 100

Proportional mortality from a particular disease = ( Number of deaths from a specific disease in a year/ Total deaths from all causes in a year ) x 100

Under 5 mortality rate = ( Number of deaths under 5 yrs of age in a year/Total live birth in that year ) x 1000

Survival rate = ( Total number of patients alive after 5 yrs /Total number of patients diagnosed or treated ) x 100

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The heart of the activated sludge process is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aeration tank

The activated sludge process is a part of the secondary sewage treatment and the heart of this process is the aeration tanks.

Pearl PF1009: Modern Sewage Treatment

Primary treatment

* Screening

* A large metal screen is used to intercept large floating objects like dead animals, wood, rags, etc., so as to prevent clogging

* Grit chamber

* It is also called detritus chamber

* It allows for the settlement of heavier solids like gravel or sand and permits the organic matter to flow through

* The grit that is collected at the bottom is then disposed of.

* Primary sedimentation

* In a primary sedimentation tank, sewage is allowed to flow slowly so that suspended matter is sediments to form sludge which is then removed without disturbing the rest of the operation.

* Biological action takes place here and breaks down complex organic solids

* Scum in the form of grease and fat collect on top of the tank

* Sometimes, chemicals like lime are added to the effluent to enhance precipitation

Secondary treatment

* Trickling filter method

* The trickling or percolating filter is a bed of crushed stones or clinker

*  Effluent from the primary sedimentation tank is spread over the filter bed and as it percolates through it, it gets oxidized by bacterial flora. There is no actual filtration that occurs.

* The oxidized sewage forms a light green material called humus and it is then led into secondary sedimentation tanks.

* Activated sludge process

* This is done in place of the trickling filter method. Both are not done together

* The heart of the activated sludge process is the aeration tank

* In these tanks, the effluent from primary sedimentation is mixed with activated or return sludge (sludge from the final settling tank) and is then exposed to aeration for 6 to 8 hours.

* During aeration, organic matter is oxidized into carbon dioxide, nitrates and water with the help of aerobic bacteria in the activated sludge.

* Secondary sedimentation

* From the trickling filters or aeration tanks, the oxidized sewage is allowed into a secondary sedimentation tank where it is held for 2 – 3 hours.

* Here, aerated sludge or activated sludge is formed, part of which is pumped back into an aeration tank

* Sludge digestion

* Sludge digestion can be done by incubating it under favorable conditions to allow anaerobic auto-digestion. This is done in sludge digestion tanks.

* Disposal of sludge is also done by sea disposal

* Sludge can also be disposed of by composting with solid refuse

* Disposal of effluent

* Disposal of effluent can be done by dilution in water bodies which has to then be chlorinated

* Disposal on land is possible if the effluent can be used for irrigation purposes

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What does the term "tracking" refer to in relation to blood pressure?
options: Observing changes in blood pressure throughout a 24-hour period
Recording and analyzing blood pressure levels over an extended period to identify patterns and predict future readings
Comparing blood pressure values between different populations based on demographics
Assessing blood pressure during exercise to evaluate cardiovascular health
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Recording and analyzing blood pressure levels over an extended period to identify patterns and predict future readings

"Tracking" in relation to blood pressure refers to recording and analyzing blood pressure levels over an extended period to identify patterns and predict future readings.

When blood pressure levels are observed from childhood through to adulthood, individuals with higher blood pressure early on typically maintain higher levels, while those with lower levels tend to stay lower as they age. This consistent ranking of blood pressure over time is called "tracking." This helps identify children and adolescents who are at risk of developing hypertension in the future.

Although blood pressure is known to increase with age in both sexes, some communities have been identified, whose mean blood pressure does not rise with age. This is because their salt intake and calorie consumption are at a subsistence level.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the level of prevention when a person receives penicillin injections for the treatment of rheumatic heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Secondary

Receiving penicillin injections for the treatment of rheumatic heart disease is Secondary prevention.

Secondary prevention includes early disease detection, and its target is healthy-appearing individuals with subclinical forms of the disease. This is defined as the action which halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications.

Levels of Prevention :

1. Primordial prevention:

* Involves the prevention of the emergence or development of risk factors in countries or population groups in which they have not yet appeared.

* Examples include adult health problems like obesity and hypertension, which have an early onset due to lifestyles like smoking, eating patterns and physical exercise, which are discouraged from early childhood

* The main intervention in primordial prevention is through individual and mass education.

2. Primary prevention:

* These are defined as "action taken prior to the onset of disease, which removes the possibility that a disease will ever occur''

* It signifies intervention in the pre-pathogenesis phase of a disease or health problem

* Primary prevention is accomplished by measures promoting general health and well-being, and the quality of life of people by specific protective measures.

* They include two strategies:

* Population (mass) strategy: Where the target group is the whole population

* High-risk strategy: Where the target group is limited to the people who are most at risk of developing a particular disease

* Examples: immunity, sanitation, and protection of food.

3. Secondary prevention :

* This is defined as "action which halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications.".

* The specific interventions are early diagnoses like screening tests and adequate treatment.

* The main aim of secondary prevention is to arrest the disease process.

* Secondary prevention is largely the domain of clinical medicine and health programs initiated by governments.

* It is an imperfect tool in the control of the transmission of disease. It is often more expensive and less effective than primary prevention.

4. Tertiary prevention :

* Measures to reduce the duration of mental illness and family and community stresses to prevent further breakdown and disruption.

* Disability limitation belongs to tertiary prevention.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the minimum per capita space required for each worker according to the Factory Act?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 500 cu ft

The minimum per capita space required for each worker according to the Factory Act is 500 cu ft.

The Factories Act, 1948 states the following in the matters of Safety and Welfare measures:

* > 1000 Workers in a factory – the appointment of 'Safety Officers'

* > 500 Workers – there should be a Welfare Officer

* > 250 Workers – a canteen shall be provided

* > 30 female workers- Crèche

According to the Indian Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: Effective as of the 1st of July 2017, mandatory crèche (daycare) facilities for every establishment employing 50 or more employees (inclusive of males and females). As this act is more recent, it supersedes the Factory Act, 1948 with regards to the requirement for a crèche.

Maximum hours of work per week including overtime work hours is 60 hours.

Pearl PF1016: The Factories act, 1948 and The Maternity Act, 2017

The Factories act,1948

* The act defines factory as an establishment employing 10 or more workers where power is used, and 20 or more workers where power is not used.

* Age of employment –  prohibition children of < 14 years from working.

* Adolescents between 15 – 18 years

* Can be employed  only in certain industries and  work between 6 AM – 7 PM

* They should not be made to work for more than four and a half hours

* They are allowed to take leave once in every 15 days and have an accumulated leave of up to 40 days

* Hours of work for adults: maximum hours of work for an industrial worker should be not more than 48 hours per week, not exceeding 9 hours a day, if working overtime then it should be no more than 60 hrs per week

* Per capita space availability: For factories established after 1948 – min 500cuft / person

* Safety and Welfare measures:

* > 1000 Workers – Safety officer

* > 500 Workers – Welfare officer

* > 250 Workers – Canteen

* > 50 Workers- Crèche*

The Maternity Act, 2017 is a landmark law which has enhanced the duration of paid maternity leave:

* Working mothers- 12 weeks to 26 weeks

* Working mothers, already with 2 surviving children - 12 weeks

* Adopting mother and commissioning mothers- 12 weeks from the date on which the child is being handed over to the mother.

*for fifty women worker after the 1976 amendment.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which is the new online software launched under the national tuberculosis elimination program (NTEP) by the government to monitor TB patients?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NIKSHAY

NIKSHAY is a web-based solution for monitoring TB patients. (The word is a combination of two Hindi words NI and KSHAY, meaning eradication of TB).

Nikshay is a web-based solution for monitoring TB patients to monitor the Revised National Tuberculosis Programme (RNTCP). This system stores information about the patient, medical history, diagnosis, co-morbidities and lab reports.

The system has been developed jointly by the Central TB Division of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and National Informatics Centre (NIC) and it was launched by the Government of India in June 2012. This is used by health functionaries at various levels across the country in association with Central TB Division (CTD), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.

NIKSHAY covers various aspects of controlling TB using technological innovations.

Apart from web-based technology, SMS services have been used effectively for communication with patients and monitoring the program on a day-to-day basis.

Other options:

Option B: Nikusth is the new online software for monitoring leprosy patients.

Option C: Nischay is a pregnancy test kit.

Option D: Axshya is a project that works to improve access to quality TB care and control through a partnership between the government and civil society.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a category C bioterrorism agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hanta virus

Hanta virus is a category C bioterrorism agent. All the other options are category A agents.

Bioterrorism refers to the intentional release of a harmful agent by attackers to cause diseases or fatalities within the human population or impact food crops and livestock. The aim is to instil fear among civilians or influence governmental actions.

As per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the agents associated with bioterrorism are grouped into three distinct categories, namely A, B and C. There is no designated Category D within this classification.

Emerging pathogens such as Hantavirus and Nipah are examples of category C bioterrorism agents.In the future, these pathogens might be modified to potentially spread widely. Their risk is increased by the following factors:

* Ease of production and dissemination

* High morbidity and mortality rates

* Ready availability

Hantaviruses, classified under Bunyaviridae, are rodent-borne viruses primarily transmitted through inhalation of the virus present in the dried excreta of rodents. It causes haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is caused by exposure to cotton dust?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Byssinosis

Byssinosis is caused by exposure to cotton dust.

Byssinosis is an occupational disease due to chronic exposure to cotton dust as in textile and rope-making industries. Chest X-ray shows hyperlucency, diaphragmatic flattening, and emphysema. A chest CT demonstrates ground glass opacities largely distributed in the basal regions with centrilobular nodules.

Other options :

Option A: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. Initially, it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis with little or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis which is called complicated coal workers' pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Option B: Silicosis is a form of pneumoconiosis which is a cause of permanent disability and mortality. It occurs in people working in sandblasting, pottery, and ceramics industry, mining, and construction work. It occurs due to the inhalation of silica dust. The patient presents with a cough, exertional dyspnea, and chest pain.

Option D: Bagassosis is an occupational lung disease caused by the inhalation of bagasse or sugarcane dust. A thermophilic actinomycete, Thermoactinomyces sacchari is the causative organism. The symptoms are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and fever. Initially, it can result in acute diffuse bronchiolitis, If left untreated it can progress to diffuse fibrosis, emphysema, and bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 64-year-old man from a village in Assam presents with genu valgum and requires a stick for walking. He reports that many other elderly individuals in his village have similar complaints. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the investigation?
options: Collect and analyze water sample for fluoride content
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Collect and analyze water sample for fluoride content

The clinical scenario of an elderly man presenting with genu valgum, along with reports of similar complaints among other elderly individuals in his village, strongly suggests an endemic cause such as skeletal fluorosis. Hence the next step in investigation is the collection and analysis of the water sample in his village for the fluoride content.

Fluorosis occurs when drinking water contains excess amounts of fluorine, in the range of 3-5mg/L. It is endemic in parts of India.

Symptoms correspond to levels of fluoride intake:

* Dental fluorosis: (1.5mg/L) Occurs if excess fluoride is ingested during the period of tooth calcification, i.e. in the first 7 years of life. Best seen on the upper incisors and almost exclusively affects only permanent teeth. It causes mottling on dental enamel, the appearance of chalky-white patches on the teeth, and loss of shine in the early stages. The white spots progressively turn yellow and can even become brown-black. The loss of enamel gives a corroded appearance.

* Skeletal fluorosis: (3-6mg/L) Occurs due to the heavy deposition of fluoride in the skeleton. Fluorosis stimulates osteoblastic activity, fluorapatite crystals are laid down in bone and these are usually resistant to secondary osteoclastic resorption. This leads to calcium retention, osteosclerosis, and osteophytosis. Ossification of ligaments and fascial attachments is characteristic.

* Crippling fluorosis: (>10mg/L) Can lead to permanent disability.

Genu valgum and osteoporosis of the lower limb are seen in a newer form of fluorosis in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. It is seen in people consuming jawar (sorghum), as it promotes greater retention of ingested fluoride.

Interventions for Fluorosis:

* Change the drinking water source with a lower fluoride content (0.5 to 0.8 mg/L). Running surface water contains lower quantities of fluorides than groundwater sources.

* The National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur developed a technique for removing fluoride by a chemical treatment called the Nalgonda technique.

* Fluoride supplements should not be prescribed for children who drink fluoridated water.

* The use of fluoride toothpaste in areas of endemic fluorosis is not recommended for children up to 6 years of age

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A chronic smoker who has worked in a cement factory for 20 years presents with mesothelioma. Which occupational exposure is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asbestosis

The clinical vignette of a person presenting with mesothelioma and a history of occupational exposure to asbestos fibers (cement factory) points towards the diagnosis of asbestosis.

Mesothelioma is strongly associated with asbestos exposure.

Asbestos-related diseases include:

* Localized fibrous plaques or diffuse pleural fibrosis

* Pleural effusion

* Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis)

* Lung carcinoma

* Mesotheliomas

* Laryngeal, ovarian and colon carcinomas

Asbestosis:

* Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis that occurs after 5-10 years of exposure to asbestos. However, once established, it progresses even in the further removal of the worker from its contact. Asbestosis affects the basal part of the lung causing diffuse peribronchial fibrosis.

* Asbestos is of 2 types i.e Serpentine/Chrysolite variety and Amphibole type

* Amphibole type has the following varieties:

* Crocidolite(blue)

* Amosite(brown)

* Anthrophyllite(white)

* Sputum shows asbestos body, which are asbestos fibres coated with fibrin.

* They present with cough and exertional dyspnoea and predominantly affects the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

* Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis typically shows a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity.

* X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones. HRCT shows subpleural fibrotic lines, irregular opacities, traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing. Lung parenchymal involvement occurs after years of exposure (at least 10 years).

Other options:

Option B:Silicosis is caused by exposure to silica dust, typically seen in mining and stone-cutting.

Option C: Farmers lung is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by inhalation of moldy hay.

Option D: Bagassosis occurs due to inhalation of bagasse (sugarcane dust)

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A Community Health Centre (CHC) receives a supply of 30 vaccine vials. Out of these, 3 vials (2 vials of Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccine and 1 vial of Pentavalent vaccine) are already opened and maintained under proper cold chain conditions. The Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM) prepares to administer these vaccines. What will she do according to the open vial policy?
options: Use MR vaccine and discard Pentavalent vaccine
Use Pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Use Pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine

According to the open vial policy, the ANM can use the pentavalent vaccine and discard the MR vaccine.

Open vial policy allows for the reuse of partially used multidose vials of applicable vaccines under the Universal Immunization Programme in subsequent sessions for up to 4 weeks, subject to certain conditions and thereby reducing vaccine wastage.

It is applicable only for DPT, TT, hepatitis B vaccine, OPV and liquid pentavalent vaccine. It is not applicable for BCG, measles, rotavirus vaccines and JE vaccines.

Vaccine vials opened in session-site can be use in more than one session up to four weeks if expiry date has not passed, if storage and transport was appropriate, no contamination has occurred in vial septum, asepsis in withdrawing was practiced and if vaccine vial monitor has not reached the discard point.

* Open vials should not be submerged in water.

* Ensure all opened vials have the recorded date and time of opening.

* At the end of a session, all vaccines should be returned to the cold chain point and segregated as reusable and non-reusable.

* All open vials of BCG, measles and JE must be destroyed after 48 hours or before the next session, whichever is earlier.

* In case of any adverse events following immunization, all open vials should not be discarded until investigation is complete.

* All vials must be transported in zipper bags in the vaccine carrier and recorded in the stock register.

* Ice packs used should be well-sealed.

Pearl PF0969: Vaccine Vial Monitors

* Vaccine vial monitors are used to monitor heat exposure of vaccines.

* It is a chemical indicator that records the cumulative heat exposure through a gradual change in color.

* If the color of the inner square is the same color or darker than the outer circle, it indicates that the vaccine has been exposed to too much heat and it must be discarded.

* Currently, there are four types of VVMs (VVM2, VVM7, VVM14, and VVM30). They are chosen to match the heat sensitivity of the vaccine.

* The VVM can be located on the label of the vaccine or on the neck or cap of the ampule/vial.

* VVMs also help in reduction of vaccine wastage by indicating which batch of vaccines can be used first.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A factory worker sustained burns involving 25% of his body while on duty. He later developed infections and related complications. Under the ESI Act, which of the following benefits is he entitled to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extended Sickness benefit

The patient developed a long-term complication (infections after burns) due to a serious condition, and under the ESI Act, such chronic or prolonged illnesses fall under the category of extended sickness benefit.

Extended sickness benefit covers those with more than 20% burns with infection or complication. Leave is given up to a maximum period of two years. The diseases for which extended sickness benefits are applied are TB, leprosy, empyema, HIV, malignancies, plegias, etc. During this period, 80 per cent of the wages are paid.

ESI act was amended to provide cash and medical benefits to employees during sickness, maternity, and employment injury. People with monthly earnings up to 21,000 are covered under this scheme. Cash benefits are made through branches and cash offices. The medical benefits are made available through ESI dispensaries, clinics, hospitals, etc. The benefits provided to the insured persons are:

* Medical benefits - Complete medical care is provided to the insured person and his/ her family members.

* Sickness benefits - include a periodic cash payment for 91 days to the insured sick person. 70% of the average daily wages is given as the daily rate if the person is under medical treatment.

* Enhanced sickness benefit - includes 14 days of leave given for tubectomy and 7 days of leave for vasectomy. The amount payable is equal to the full wages.

* Maternity benefits - cash payments equal to full wages are paid to the insured person for up to 26 weeks in cases of pregnancy.

* Disablement benefit - cash payment and free medical treatment are given for temporary or permanent disablements and occupational diseases.

* Dependant's benefit - if an employment injury causes the death of the insured person, the dependants are eligible for periodic payments.

* Funeral expenses of Rs 15000 are payable to the dependants.

* Rehabilitation allowance - the insured person and the family members continue to get medical treatment after permanent disablement and retirement.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A girl with a history of schizophrenia presents to a Primary Health Centre (PHC). Which of the following online government portals should the doctor use to book an appointment with a psychiatrist?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tele - MANAS

Tele-MANAS (Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States) is the flagship online platform that provides access to mental health services, enabling doctors and frontline health workers to connect patients directly to psychiatrists and trained mental health professionals for consultation.

Tele MANAS, a 24/7 mental health support helpline, launched its mobile app and video consultation services to enhance access to mental health support.

The Tele MANAS app is a user-friendly platform that offers a range of mental health resources. Users can access self-care tips, stress management techniques, and tools for recognizing early signs of distress. The app also features interactive activities, including mind challenges, games, and mindfulness practices. Additionally, Tele MANAS provides free, confidential counseling with trained mental health professionals from across India.

Video consultations enhance the already existing audio call services, enabling mental health professionals to conduct thorough assessments through direct observation. This feature facilitates history taking, clarification of concerns, and brief physical or Mental State Examinations (MSE) when needed. The service is initially available in Karnataka, Jammu & Kashmir, and Tamil Nadu, with plans for nationwide expansion.

Tele MANAS services include:

* Immediate tele-counselling by trained professionals.

* Referral support to psychiatrists for severe cases.

* Mental health awareness campaigns via digital platforms.

* Mobile-based mental health interventions ensure accessibility in rural and remote areas.

Other Options:

Option A: NIKSHAY is a digital platform for the management of tuberculosis cases.

Option C: U-WIN is a digital platform for recording all vaccination-related activities and tracking the administration of vaccines under Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).

Option D: Nikusth is the web-based solution for monitoring of Leprosy patients

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A group of experts delivered speeches one by one, with no discussion allowed between them, and at the end, one person summarized the key points. What is this type of academic session called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Symposium

A symposium is method of health communication and it comprises of a series of speeches on the topic with the chairman summarizing at the end.

A symposium is a series of speeches on a selected subject by experts. Each expert presents an aspect of the subject briefly, after which the audience is allowed to ask questions. There is no discussion among symposium members. The chairman makes a comprehensive summary at the end of the session.

Option D - Panel discussions take place with 4-8 qualified persons who sit together and discuss a topic in front of an audience. It has a chairman, moderator, and 4-8 speakers. There is no specific agenda or set speeches. The audience is also invited to take part after the main discussion.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A group of students who were mainly consuming khesari dal and rice water developed weakness in their legs. On examination, their legs moved in a crossed manner while walking, and some were seen walking on their toes. Which of the following vitamin prophylaxis could have prevented this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

The clinical scenario of students consuming mainly khesari dal and rice water and later presenting with weakness of legs and scissor-like walking(crossed legs) gait is suggestive of neurolathyrism. Vitamin C in doses of 500-1000mg can be used for the prevention and treatment of lathyrism.

Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals. It is due to the consumption of Khesari dal/Lathyrus sativus or its variants such as sweet pea(Lathyrus odoratus). It is mostly consumed by agricultural labourers of poor economic status because it is relatively cheap. It can present as skeletal, vascular, or neural manifestations.

It usually affects young males aged 15-45 years and it is manifested in stages:

* Latent stage: The individual is apparently healthy, but when subjected to a physical ungainly gait. if the pulse is withdrawn from the diet, it will result in complete remission of the disease.

* No-stick stage: the patient walks with short, jerky steps without the aid of a stick.

* One-stick stage: The patient walks with a crossed gait and a tendency to walk on toes. stick is used for balance due to muscular stiffness.

* Two-stick stage: Due to excessive bending of knees and crossed legs, the patient needs two crutches for support. The gait is slow and clumsy and the patient gets tired easily after walking a short distance.

* Crawler stage: Finally, the erect posture becomes impossible as the knee joints cannot support the weight of the body. The patient is reduced to crawling by throwing his weight on his hands.

The patient is initially able to walk with short jerky steps without any aids, but the progressive spastic paralysis causes a crossed gait, and the patient has to use sticks to maintain his balance. Eventually, the knee joints are unable to support the weight of the body and the patient cannot stand erect at all. Long-term consumption of khesari dal leads to neurolathyrism. It is characterized by gradual spastic paralysis of the lower limbs.

The interventions that can be used to prevent lathyrism include:

* Vitamin C prophylaxis.

* Limiting the proportion of the dal to less than a quarter of the total cereals and pulses consumed in a day.

* Removal of the toxin by parboiling and steeping method.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A lady with her 9-month-old baby presented to the doctor asking for another BCG vaccine dose for her child, as there is no visible BCG vaccination scar. The doctor checked the vaccination card and confirmed that the birth dose was given. The Mantoux test was done and came back negative. What is the next step?
options: BCG vaccination at 12 months of age
Do Mantoux test and wait for the result
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reassurance to mother

After BCG vaccination, the presence of a scar is not a reliable indicator of protection. Some children may not develop a visible scar despite receiving the vaccine. Therefore, the mother should simply be reassured.

Since the vaccination card confirms that the birth dose of BCG was given, and the Mantoux test is negative, no repeat BCG dose is required.

BCG (bacillus of Calmette and Guerin) is the only live bacterial vaccine. The WHO has recommended the Danish 1331 strain for the production of the BCG vaccine. It protects against severe forms of childhood tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis. It also reduces morbidity and mortality from primary tuberculosis.

There are two types of BCG vaccine: the liquid (fresh) vaccine and the freeze-dried vaccine. The freeze-dried vaccine is a more stable preparation (option B) than the liquid vaccine. Currently, the vaccine is distributed in the freeze-dried form because of better storage qualities. Normal saline is recommended for reconstituting the vaccine, as distilled water may cause irritation. The reconstituted vaccine may be used up within 3 hours.

The usual strength for vaccination is 0.1 mg in 0.1 ml volume. The dose given at birth (option A) and for newborns < 4 weeks of age is 0.05 ml. It is injected intradermally (option C) just above the insertion of the left deltoid muscle using a tuberculin syringe.

Other options:

Option B and C: BCG revaccination is not included in the official immunisation schedule in India under the expanded programme on immunization.

Option D: Mantoux test is already done and is negative, so no further action is needed.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A long-term study found that individuals with high blood pressure (BP) during childhood continued to have high BP in adulthood, while those with low BP in childhood tended to maintain lower levels later in life. Which epidemiological concept does this pattern best represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tracking of blood pressure

The above phenomenon is best described as the "tracking" of blood pressure.

In this phenomenon, the blood pressure of individuals is followed up from early childhood into adulthood. The BP in individuals with low BP levels tend to remain low, and in those with high BP levels, they tend to remain high. This phenomenon of persistence of rank order of blood pressure has been described as "tracking". This is helpful in identifying children and adolescents who are at risk of developing hypertension in their future.

Other options:

Option A: The rule of halves depicts the disease burden of hypertension in the community. It states that only about half of the hypertensive subjects in the general population are aware of the condition. Only half of those aware are being treated and only half of those being treated are considered to be adequately treated.

A pictorial representation of the rule of halves in hypertension is shown below:

Option C: The cohort effect is a concept used in social science and epidemiology, particularly when studying changes in populations over time. It refers to the variations or trends in a particular characteristic or outcome that are observed in a group (cohort) due to their shared experiences and exposures during a specific time period.

Option D: Regression to the mean describes the statistical tendency of extreme values to move closer to the average upon repeated measurement

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A man working as a mason in a Kota stone factory presents with dyspnea and has following chest X-ray findings. Which occupational exposure is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Silicosis

A patient with dyspnea and eggshell calcifications on chest X-ray, combined with a history of occupational exposure to silica dust, is strongly suggestive of silicosis.

Silicosis is an occupational disease and is caused by exposure to silica. It is seen in people who work in mining, stone cutting, sandblasting, and quarrying.It is the most common pneumoconiosis in the world. In silicosis, macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-8) that cause fibroblast recruitment.

In simple silicosis, the chest X-ray shows small rounded opacities in the upper lobes. When there is progressive nodular fibrosis, irregular masses >1 cm are seen, referred to as complicated silicosis. When these masses enlarge further, it is called progressive massive fibrosis (PMF). Calcification of hilar lymph nodes leads to the appearance of eggshell calcification. Silicosis increases the risk of lung cancer. It also increases susceptibility to tuberculosis as pulmonary macrophages are inhibited from killing the phagocytosed mycobacteria by crystalline silica.

Other options:

Option B: Asbestosis occurs due to the inhalation of crystalline hydrated silicates (asbestos). It is characterized by diffuse parenchymal interstitial fibrosis.

Option C:Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis

Option D: Tuberculosis is a specific infectious disease caused by M. tuberculosis. The disease primarily affects lungs and causes pulmonary tuberculosis. It can also affect intestine, meninges, bones and joints, lymph glands, skin and other tissues of the body.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with cancer and is undergoing chemotherapy. What type of prevention is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tertiary prevention

The clinical scenario of a patient diagnosed with cancer and undergoing chemotherapy points towards tertiary prevention, as it is already diagnosed and treatment aimed at reducing the number and impact of complications.

The tertiary level of prevention signifies intervention in the late pathogenesis phase. Tertiary prevention can be defined as "all measures available to reduce or limit impairments and disabilities, minimize suffering caused by existing departures from good health, and promote the patient's adjustment to irremediable conditions". Examples include occupational and physical therapy in burns patients and cardiac rehabilitation in post-myocardial infarction patients.

Other options:

Option A: Secondary prevention includes early disease detection and targets healthy-looking individuals with subclinical forms of the disease. Secondary prevention is defined by an intervention that halts the progress of the disease at its incipient stage and prevents complications. A Papanicolaou (Pap) smear is an example of secondary prevention aimed at diagnosing cervical cancer in its subclinical state before progression.

Option C: Primordial prevention prevents the emergence or development of risk factors in population groups or countries where they have not appeared yet through individual and mass education. For example lifestyle modifications such as eating patterns and physical exercise to prevent obesity in later years.

Option D: Primary prevention is the action taken before the onset of the disease to prevent the possibility that a disease will ever occur. Here, intervention is initiated in the pre-pathogenesis phase of a disease. It is accomplished by population strategy and high-risk strategy. Examples of primary prevention are immunization and sanitising hands.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of increased consumption of bajra (pearl millet) roti now presents with complaints of drowsiness and giddiness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ergotism

The clinical scenario of a patient presenting with drowsiness and giddiness following increased consumption of bajra is highly indicative of ergotism.

Ergot or Claviceps purpurae is a field fungus. Food grains like bajra, rye, sorghum, and wheat have a tendency to get contaminated with this ergot fungus. It grows as a blackish mass and the seeds become black and irregular(refer to image below). These get harvested along with the food grains and consumption of this ergot-infested grain leads to ergotism.

Acute cases present with nausea, vomiting, giddiness, and drowsiness for a period of up to 24 to 48 hours after the ingestion of ergot grain. In cases of chronic consumption, they present with painful cramps in limbs, and peripheral gangrene due to vasoconstriction of capillaries.

Ergot-infested grains can be removed easily by floating them in 20 percent saltwater. Floatation and handpicking can also be used for the removal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient with leprosy received treatment for 4 months but then discontinued it for 1 year. Now, the patient presents again with a skin lesion. What should be the next step in management?
options: Start treatment with the new pack and new schedule
Continue the old treatment and give the remaining doses
Increase the dosage for the time being and then continue the old regimen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Start treatment with the new pack and new schedule

When a patient discontinues leprosy treatment for such a long duration (1 year), the case is treated as a treatment default. In such situations, WHO/NLEP guidelines recommend restarting the entire full course of  the multidrug therapy(MDT).

A defaulter who returns to the health centre for treatment should be given a new course of MDT when he or she shows signs such as reddish and/or raised skin lesions, appearance of new skin lesions since the previous examination, new nerve involvement, lepromatous nodules, or signs of reversal reaction.

Leprosy is managed based on the bacterial load. According to revised diagnostic and treatment criteria, WHO defines paucibacillary (PB) disease as the presence of no bacilli on smears or biopsy and less than or equal to 5 skin lesions with no peripheral nerve involved. Multibacillary (MB) leprosy is characterised by bacilli on smears or biopsies of more than 5 skin lesions and more than or equal to 1 peripheral nerve involvement.

WHO currently recommends treating PB leprosy with a combination of 3 drugs—rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine—for 6 months. Meanwhile, MB leprosy is treated using the same 3 drugs for 12 months. While the NLEP guidelines earlier mentioned a 2-drug MDT for PB leprosy, the National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy (2023-2027) now recommends a uniform MDT of 3 drugs for both PB and MB leprosy.

Chemoprophylaxis for leprosy should be given in:

* Contacts who are more than 2 years

* Those with close contact with the patient for more than 20 hours per week for more than 3 months

A single dose of rifampicin is recommended for the close contact of a patient with leprosy provided they do not develop any signs or symptoms pertaining to leprosy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person is planning to move from Nigeria to the USA. He is advised to have a vaccine certificate that is valid. Which vaccine certificate will be validated by the US Embassy for VISA purposes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 17D vaccine

The International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005) mandate that travellers from endemic countries (such as Nigeria) must produce a valid yellow fever vaccination certificate when entering countries like the USA.

The strain used for the yellow fever vaccination is the 17D vaccine. The 17D vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine, administered subcutaneously.  It is valid for a lifetime beginning 10 days after vaccination.  The incubation period of yellow fever is 3–6 days. Unvaccinated people are required to remain quarantined for 6 days (maximum period of incubation).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted among nursing staff to analyze the time spent on different aspects of patient care, including bed preparation, monitoring vital signs, attending doctors’ rounds, blood sampling, and drug administration. Which of the following management techniques is most appropriate for this type of analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Work sampling

The management technique that is being applied for the above study is work sampling.

Work sampling is a quantitative management technique. It refers to the systematic observation and recording of the activities of one or more individuals. It is done at predetermined or random intervals. It mainly includes analyzing the type of activities performed and the time needed to perform the same.

These studies have been done on doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and laboratory technicians. This technique can find the appropriateness of the current staff, job description, and training. This may standardize the methods of performing activities and determine the manpower needed in an organization.

Management is the purposeful and effective use of resources such as manpower, materials, and finances for the fulfillment of a pre-determined objective. They consist of four basic activities: planning, organizing, communicating, and monitoring.

Management techniques are of two types:

Quantitative methods

Methods based on behavioral sciences

• Cost-Effective analysis
• Cost-Accounting
• Input-Output analysis
• Model
• Systems analysis
• Network analysis

• Program Evaluation and Review Technique (PERT)
• Critical Path Method (CPM)

• Planning–Programming–Budgeting System (PPBS)

Other options:

Option A: Network analysis is a systematic approach used to plan, organize, and manage complex projects by breaking them down into interconnected tasks. It helps in identifying the sequence of activities, estimating time requirements, and optimizing resource allocation.

Option C: Critical pathway method is a type of network analysis technique. The longest path in the network is called the critical path. If any delay in activity along the critical pathway, the entire study will be delayed.

Option D: Systems analysis is a quantitative method of management. Systems analysis helps decision-makers by identifying the problem, setting objectives, exploring and evaluating alternative solutions for cost-effectiveness, and reviewing objectives when necessary.

questions.text: A study was conducted in a school where information regarding vaccination status, gender of students, and their pain scale scores was collected. Mention the types of data taken in the same sequence?

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted on workers in an aniline dye factory. One group consisted of workers exposed to the dye, and the other group included clerical staff with no exposure. All relevant information was collected from factory records spanning the past 20 years. What type of study does this represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retrospective study

Factory workers exposed to aniline dye were compared with clerical staff using records from the past 20 years. Since both the exposure and outcomes had already occurred, and the study moved forward from those past records to analyze disease occurrence, it points towards a retrospective cohort study.

A cohort study progresses from cause (exposure) to effect (disease).

* Types of cohort study:

* Prospective (concurrent) cohort studies

* Retrospective (historical) cohort studies

* Combination cohort studies

* Steps of cohort study:

* Selection of study subjects

* Obtaining data on exposure

* Selection of comparison groups

* Follow-up

* Analysis in terms of incidence rates and estimation of risk

* Advantages of cohort study:

* Incidence can be calculated

* Several possible outcomes related to exposure can be studied at the same time

* Provides direct estimate of relative risk

* Calculation of dose-response ratio

* Minimization of certain biases

* Disadvantages of cohort study:

* Cannot use for uncommon diseases

* Expensive, requires a large population and longer time

* Many common administrative and ethical problems

* High attrition and selection of subjects is difficult

* Dynamism of diagnostics is difficult to incorporate

* Tends to alter the behaviour of subjects known as Hawthorne effect.

Other options:

Option A: In a case-control study, the study begins with the outcome and goes retrospectively to find out the exposure among the cases and controls.For example, to find the exposure to smoking associated with already diagnosed lung cancer patients.

Option B: An ecological study is any kind of study in which data is collected about a population and is analyzed at that level. Unlike the case with cohort studies, in these studies, no data is available or analyzed about individuals.

Option D: A cross-sectional study Is an observational study used to calculate a disease's distribution and prevalence.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A young male, whose diet predominantly consists of rice and pulses, presents with fatigue and mild neuropathy. The family also consumes the same diet. Which supplementation should be given to the family for prophylaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

The given clinical scenario of a young male who consumes rice as a staple diet and presents with fatigue and neuropathy points to the diagnosis of Beri-beri.

The vitamin deficiency associated with this condition is thiamine (vitamin B1). It is commonly seen in people who consume polished rice-based monotonous diets. Hence, thiamine supplementation should be started for the prevention of Beri-Beri.  Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

The two principal deficiency diseases of thiamine are:

* Beriberi may occur in three main forms :

* The dry form is characterized by nerve involvement (peripheral neuritis)

* The wet form is characterized by heart involvement (cardiac beriberi)

* The infantile form: The affected infant is typically breast-fed by a thiamine-deficient mother. The mother often exhibits clinical features of peripheral neuropathy. It is usually seen at 2 to 4 months of age

* Wernicke's encephalopathy is often seen often in alcoholics. It is characterized by ophthalmoplegia, polyneuritis, ataxia and mental deterioration. It occurs occasionally in people who fast.

High-risk groups for thiamine deficiency are:

* Lactating mothers

* Patients on regular haemodialysis

* Persistent vomiting

* Prolonged gastric aspiration

* People who go on long fasts

High-risk groups should be treated with direct supplementation of thiamine.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per Biomedical Waste Management guidelines, cotton swabs used for cleaning a wound contaminated with pus and maggots should be disposed of in which color-coded bag?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yellow non chlorinated bag

Cotton swabs used for cleaning wounds contaminated with blood, pus, or body fluids are categorized under “soiled waste,” which the guidelines specify should be disposed of in yellow-colored non-chlorinated plastic bag.

According to biomedical waste management guidelines, soiled waste items such as dressings, plaster casts, cotton swabs, and bags containing residual or discarded blood and blood components must be collected in yellow bags and treated by incineration, plasma pyrolysis, or deep burial.

Other options:

Option A and B: Red bags are used for contaminated recyclable wastes like tubing, intravenous tubes and sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes(without needles, and gloves).

Option D: Yellow chlorinated bags are not recommended, as the guideline specifies non-chlorinated yellow bags.
